speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to congratulate you and particularly commend the fact that for the first time in our history we have a Speaker of the House of Commons who is genuinely the choice of all Members and not simply the choice of the Government of the day. I believe we all have a responsibility to try to restore the sense of purpose and decorum of this Chamber. I for one share that sense of responsibility. I believe we can restore decorum in this Chamber without harming Parliament's ability to make the Government accountable and to ensure that the differences of the three Parties are put forward.
I have to say that I regret the kind of tactics we have just seen in the House which are incomprehensible to average Canadians, but if average Canadians could understand on what we have wasted half an hour of the House's time, they would find those tactics juvenile, infantile and demeaning.

subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I want to begin by saying a word to my constituents in Ottawa Centre and to all of the other federal employees who are affected by the Government's restraints on their political rights. This summer, the Charter case on political rights, which I launched in 1984, finally reached the Federal Court. Mr. Justice Walsh's decision opened the door a bit wider to political acitivity by federal employees, but in his decision Mr. Justice Walsh refused to strike down the relevant sections of the Public Service Employment Act. I have, therefore, gone to the Federal Court of Appeal in conjunction with my co-plaintiffs from the Public Service Alliance. We hope to win our points there, but I deeply regret that there was no mention of this issue in the Throne Speech. It is time the Government got this issue out of the courts and into Parliament by bringing forward legislation which we can debate and put into law as the Conservatives promised before the 1984 election.
I remain committed to winning political rights for public servants. I want to warn the Government that its record will be on the line if it does not act on its promise to provide political rights before the 1988 election.
There are two other local issues on which I would like to comment briefly, Mr. Speaker. I am extremely disturbed at the cuts announced today in the budget for the National Research Council. I have today written to all members of the board of the National Research Council urging them to do everything possible to stop those cuts, including resigning en masse if necessary. It is intolerable that the Government's decision to have a space agency and to have the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) head a committee on industrial research should be used to undermine the National Research Council at a time when everybody in Canada acknowledges the need for this country to take leadership in research and development rather than gutting the five institutions and the work that is now being done.
I want to say to you, Mr. Speaker, since you are now in office as Speaker, that I am disturbed. I hope you will make representations privately to the Government over its delays in proclaiming Bill C-45 in order to give bargaining rights to House of Commons employees. The employees feel that the delay is being put into place in order to give the Commons administration time to shake things up in a way that will be favourable to management and will disregard the rights of employees. I hope that you take that very seriously, Sir, and get Bill C-45 proclaimed as quickly as possible.

Mr. Speaker, I am delighted with the progress made by the New Democratic Party in Quebec, and I want to thank all Quebecers who have joined our ranks in increasing numbers over the past two years. Recent polls indicate that nearly one third of the population of Quebec would support the New Democratic Party in the event of a federal election and that Ed Broadbent is as popular in Quebec, as the leader of his party, as the Prime Minister. Although we have yet to win federal seats in Quebec, the NDP is ahead of the Conservatives in Quebec,
October 9, 1986

and we intend to stay ahead. The strong increase in votes for the NDP in the by-election in Saint-Maurice, hardly a promising riding for the NDP, shows the extent to which Quebecers know and support us. Is this a temporary phenomenon, arising from a case of disenchantment with the two old parties? I would say no, Mr. Speaker, because for two years, the NDP has been far more visible on the Quebec federal scene. In the House of Commons, we are asking more and more questions about matters of concern to the people of Quebec, ranging from shipyards, and the textile industry to the industrial future of Montreal East and de-indexation of Old Age Security pensions.
Since January, we have made about 50 trips in the various regions of Quebec to meet voters, militant party members, community groups, labour organizations, farmers, women's groups, and business associations. Mr. Speaker, we intend to keep up the good work. Our commitment to Quebec will continue beyond the next election, because the New Democratic Party represents and wants to represent the middle class and ordinary people, not just from British Columbia or Newfoundland or Ontario but from all over Canada, including Quebec.
Mr. Speaker, when travelling through Quebec and Ontario,
I am increasingly struck by the differences between the various regions of our country. More and more, we seem to be living in two Canadas, no longer the two solitudes of the English and French, but the two solid solitudes of rich and poor. In the urban areas of Southern Ontario, economic growth has brought unemployment down to less than 6 per cent. Not perfect, but not depression statistics either. In the rest of the country, however, there has been very little change. In Quebec, the unemployment rate has remained at 11.5 per cent. In some regions, it exceeds 20 per cent. In the private sector, according to the Conservatives, the growth rate in Southern Ontario is coming along very nicely. However, even the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Bouchard) admits that the private sector has little to offer in his region, Lac-Saint-Jean.
One month ago my Leader appointed me finance critic for the NDP here in Parliament. It is an honour and a challenge for me to take on this new responsility because economic management is central to every other issue in Government today. As I was just saying en francais, we are increasingly coming to a situation where we have two Canadas, one rich and one poor. That is an intolerable situation which I, as one spokesman for my Party, and my Party as a whole, are committed to bringing to an end.
Over the summer Canadians made it clear that they question the Conservative Government over its lack of integrity and lack of fairness. They were looking for a fresh start in the Throne Speech but they did not get it. The Speech reminded me of what I used to hear in the Ontario Legislature in the 1970s when Dalton Camp and Senator Norman Atkins were advising Premier Davis.
The Address-Mr. Cassidy
While I welcome the announcement that there will be new conflict of interest legislation as a result of the problems of the former Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion, I am disappointed that there is no other recognition in the Throne Speech that Canadians want action on what the Prime Minister and his colleagues dismiss as the small things which have troubled his Government. It is not a small thing to waste millions of dollars to give our Prime Minister the trappings of a U.S. President. The pork-barrelling that went on to move a prison from Drummondville to Manicouagan, the politicization of the top civil service which is inherent in the appointment of Dalton Camp as a senior deputy minister, the revision of events which seem to go on whenever the Prime Minister talks to the press, all these things define the style of the present Government and are major factors in its collapse in the polls.
When you look at the big things which the Government claims have been going right, you also begin to wonder about the Conservative's credibility. The number one priority for most Canadians is secure employment. Yet one and a quarter million Canadians are still officially out of work and hundreds of thousands more would be seeking work if jobs were available. We have had no growth in jobs since January of 1986, almost a whole year. Unemployment is worse in the Atlantic provinces today than it was before the 1984 election. While unemployment is as low as 5 per cent in certain parts of southern Ontario like the City of London, it is close to 10 per cent here in Ottawa in the area I represent. It is 12 per cent in many parts of Quebec, higher than that in British Columbia, and running at over 21 per cent in Newfoundland. To all intents and purposes we now have two economies in Canada, one that is starting to thrive in southern Ontario and a vast area from St. John's to Victoria which is dangerously close to depression.
John Diefenbaker cried out for one Canada, but his Conservative successors in 1986 are rapidly creating two Canadas, one for the rich and one for the poor. Last year family income in southern Ontario averaged $41,765, which is some 40 per cent more than the average family income in Newfoundland. The response of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Crosbie) to that kind of disparity is to say that people in the Atlantic provinces should be glad they do not live in Bangladesh. This is not a Third World country. I would have thought that, as the regional Minister from Newfoundland, the Minister would be talking about how he and his Government can create living conditions in Newfoundland comparable to those in Ontario rather than telling people they can eat cake.
In Canada today one million families live below the poverty line. Only 3.6 per cent of total income goes to the bottom 20 per cent of our population. People at the top of the heap, the top one-fifth of income earners, take 43.3 per cent of all income. Yet what does the Throne Speech do about that situation? What does it say about the problems within our midst? One searches in vain to even find the word "poverty" mentioned in the speech.

October 9, 1986
The Address-Mr. Cassidy
Wealthy Canadians in the corporate sector keep urging the Government to bring down the budgetary deficit. Last year the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) went to Bay Street to talk to those wealthy Canadians. He told them that even though he had miscalculated figures for the current fiscal year, he intends to stay the course and continue deficit reduction as his top priority. It is about time he realized that the view from Etobicoke and Bay Street is not the view of the average Canadian. The Government needs to respond to the needs of the average Canadian, not just those who are well off in the areas where he hangs out in southern Ontario. On behalf of millions of Canadians threatened with unemployment and job insecurity I want to know why the Government could not have used the Throne Speech to point to the unacceptably high unemployment rate of 9.7 per cent across Canada and set targets for systematically bringing that rate down rather than just setting targets for deficit reduction.
It is the same thing when you talk about taxes. In the last two years the Government increased taxes of ordinary Canadian families by $1,300 per year. At the same time it cut tax rates for corporations and the rich. Last month we released figures which show that every year some 80,000 profitable Canadian corporations, almost one-third of the total, with income in the $12 billion range, paid no corporate income tax. In some years a teller at the Royal Bank on Sparks Street in my constituency paid more income tax all by herself than her employer had to pay on assets which today total $98 billion across Canada. Is that fair? It is another sign of what I mean when I say that we now have two Canadas, one rich and one poor.
Canadians were looking for a clear sense of direction in the Throne Speech, not just the mushy generalities they got. I would like to outline what I and my Party see as priorities which should be put in place and will be put in place when the NDP forms the next Government of Canada.
The first priority should be to put jobs first and not the deficit. When the Minister of Finance announced an upward revision of the deficit, he assured his former colleagues on Bay Street that the program for deficit reduction remains in place. He has yet to give the people on Main Street his targets for reducing unemployment, and in my view he has his priorities wrong. No single move will do more to cut government costs and boost tax revenues than putting Canadians back to work. In other words, if we put jobs at the top of the priority list, that will help with the deficit picture as well. However, the way it is happening right now, we can see that the preoccupation of the Government with the deficit is reducing disposable income, reducing Canadians' willingness to buy goods and services, and is serving as a drag on the economy and making it impossible to create new jobs.
The experience of Manitoba's NDP Government when they came back to power five years ago, the experience of the NDP Government in the Yukon which halved the rate of unemployment in its first year of office, show that a Government can set
meaningful targets for reducing unemployment and can achieve them. We should be doing that here in Canada.
We should also be committed to being fair to every region and every Canadian in every part of our country. The emergence of two Canadas has got to come to an end. The idea that the prospects for someone from Cape Breton are dismal, whereas his counterpart living in southern Ontario, in Toronto, Hamilton or London, will have rosier prospects is surely intolerable and we should now bring a sense of hope and promise to people in all corners of Canada. Faced with this challenge the response of the Government has been to do nothing except tell the regions that they are going to have to pull themselves up by their own bootstraps.

Eighteen months ago, Mr. Speaker, the New Democratic Party's employment task force travelled throughout Canada seeking solutions to our unemployment problems. Our report was an endorsement of the initiative shown in various regions, the contribution of small- and medium-sized businesses, and the urgency of decentralizing programs and being flexible.
Apparently the Government has agreed to some of our recommendations, but this will prove to be a worthless exercise if no money is available to fund a new approach to regional development. The two Canadas will continue to exist but the gap between them will simply grow ever wider.
Without a commitment to equality and justice as well as decentralization and flexibility the disparities will continue, particularly if the Government continues to see its main role as allowing the private sector to make southern Ontario rich while the rest of Canada slips back into depression status.
The third issue is that of fair taxes. The Finance Department's own polls show that the vast majority of Canadians believe that the tax system is unfair. There is an emerging and growing concern about our tax system. It has become so bad and so ineffective that even the corporate sector is saying that something must be done. However, the corporate sector's solutions are becoming the Government's solutions and they are not the solutions for ordinary Canadians.
The Throne Speech says that personal income taxes will be decreased. We would welcome that, Mr. Speaker, but we know what the Finance Minister has in mind. He wants to bring in a businesss transfer tax which will be a new form of tax on consumption that will be paid by ordinary Canadians. It will replace and broaden the existing manufacturers sales tax. No matter what you call it, this is not a tax on business but rather on individuals.
It became clear from our tax probe over the course of the last year that the present system is unfair, inefficient and unaccountable, particularly when it comes to the billions of dollars of concessions given to corporations. President Reagan
October 9, 1986

and the Republicans in the United States Congress put forward a tax reform which raises corporate taxation in that country by $120 billion while reducing personal tax rates. We could have that kind of fair tax reform in Canada as well.
We need a commitment for a real war on poverty to wipe it out of Canada before the end of the century. We need a commitment for action rather than just studies and speeches to stop the needless concentration of the businesss sector which has put so much of the wealth of the country in the hands of a handful of irresponsible corporate families.

Mr. Speaker, we need a firm commitment concerning the economic equality of women in this country; more than sheer rhetoric, more than toothless legislation which will do precious little to improve the condition of working women, we need a commitment supported by Canadian legislation so that women in this country will indeed achieve real equality.

I believe that we need to talk about genuine economic democracy. It is time that we abandoned 19th century ways of organizing the workplace and conducting relations between management or employers and employees. When I talk to working people I ask them whether their employers tell them what is going on, whether they know the situation of their enterprise, firm or government Department. I ask whether they are given responsibility, whether decisions are shared in their workplace. Overwhelmingly the response is no. We are moving into the 21st century, yet businesses in Canada are still being run as though this was the 19th century.
We are in a very difficult competitive situation, not only with our friends in the United States, but with Japan, Taiwan, Korea and every other country. We have to act now to involve the abilities, the brainpower, the ingenuity and the commitment of every Canadian in that competitive battle to keep standards of living high in this country, to achieve the other priorities that I have talked about and to ensure that we have democracy, and not only in our social and political lives. By curbing the power of big business and the concentration of power we give power back to the men and women who make Canada great. That commitment in economic democracy is extremely important.
I would like to conclude by saying that there is an opportunity for another amendment to the Throne Speech. A number of themes that I have put forward are shared with me by my Party. That is why I wish to move, seconded by the Hon. Member for Kamloops-Shuswap (Mr. Riis), that the following be added to the address:
That this House regrets that the Government has failed to provide leadership on major issues of social justice affecting average Canadians including the need for action to provide greater protection for battered women, a commitment to legislate pro-rated benefits for part-time workers, the majority of whom are women, a refusal to establish and work towards lower unemployment targets for Canadians, and the failure to pursue a serious tax reform that would eliminate the unfairness, the complexity and unaccountability of the present system.
The Address-Mr. Cassidy
I ask all Hon. Members to support me in adding this amendment to the Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne which represents priorities which we feel cannot be shoved aside until 1988 or 1990 but must be addressed now.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to address a few of the points that the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Cassidy) brought up. He knows that Throne Speeches are always thematic in nature. They cannot be entirely specific. I hope he realizes that. I am very proud of the very progressive statements contained in the Throne Speech. I would like to recount a few things that have occurred which I think will be at variance with several things the Hon. Member said.
Tax reform is long overdue in this country. The Government is going to tackle some of the specific issues the Member spoke of with regard to fairness. I hope we can reduce the tax brackets. I know that we can wipe out some of the inequalities which have occurred. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) has already taken great strides in that. However that is not something that we could be very specific about in the Throne Speech.
Great strides are needed in this direction, but this is not simple. I am not sure what the exact strategy will be. It may occur in two phases. However, there is a very strong commitment on this side of the House to deliver for average Canadians. There will be a shift in the burden of taxation away from individuals and toward corporations. Major steps have already been taken to shut down some of the loopholes.
With regard to new regulatory reforms for the financial institutions, the Member has served as an alternate on the Finance Committee and knows that a very comprehensive review has already been done by the Finance and Economic Affairs Committee. I am sure that in the near future we will see some most progressive reforms in that area.
Corporate concentration is a topic on which I have spoken on a number of occasions. I share some of the Hon. Member's concerns, but I do not share his pessimism with regard to what the Government will do. The Member knows that not many months ago we brought in a new competition law which had been waiting for decades to be introduced. There is a tribunal now in place that would take care of excessive decisions that would limit competition in the market-place.
I give the Hon. Member some credit and share his view that we will need to go further as a Government because there are some 32 families in this country who control an enormous amount of wealth and we need a structure in place so that it is not abused.

October 9, 1986
The Address-Mr. Cassidy
Let me touch on a few of the social issues on which the Government is proceeding. For instance, with the exploitation of young children and women, pornography is a grave concern to many people in the country. That issue will be solved.

subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: I regret to interrupt the Hon. Member but we have already taken more than three minutes of the ten-minute period for questions and comments. I would like to allow the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Cassidy) to reply. Other Members also wish to put questions.

subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the comments of the Hon. Member because I look forward to working v/ith him since I am becoming a full member of the Finance Committee. I believe that we can work together and I hope that he will provide some leadership and drag his Government into the 21st century, since I am not sure that all of its members want to go into it.
One of the issues that I believe he should address is that when the Government talks about tax reform it forgets to mention that in the last two years the Conservatives have raised the tax by $1,300 on average Canadian families while, at the same time, reducing tax rates on corporations and giving enormous tax windfalls to very wealthy people with capital gains. If we are going to talk about tax reform, we must start by rolling back the mistakes of the last two years and put in place a tax reform that will genuinely get a fair share of tax revenues from the corporate sector. I am not convinced that the Government wants to do anything more than simply iron out inequities in taxation between corporations without ensuring that they pay a much greater and fairer share of the total tax burden.

subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to make a short comment and then ask the Hon. Member three questions. First, he was very critical of the Government's dealing with unemployment. However, he failed to point out that when the Government, in the two Budget Speeches and economic statements that have been made so far, outlined the proposal it would make to deal with the economy, the Leader of his Party stood in his place and indicated that those proposals and that type of approach would devastate the economy and put more people out of work rather than more people back to work. As the Hon. Member knows, it has had just the reverse effect. In fact, interest rates have fallen, inflation has fallen, and unemployment has fallen.
I believe that the Hon. Member should be standing in his place and applauding the Government's approach, rather than criticizing it.
However, my question relates to the aspect of tax reform to which the Hon. Member has referred. I know that the Hon. Member's Party in its NDP Tax Probe 86, has been looking very seriously at the whole situation of federal sales tax and corporate taxes. I have been most interested to read the reports from the NDP tax probe so far. However, I have yet to see what the NDP proposes specifically with respect to corporate taxes and the elimination of corporate tax expenditures. The New Democratic Party has sometimes called these tax rip-offs,
but the Finance Department calls them tax expenditures. I suspect that the NDP wants to keep some but I am not sure whether there are specific ones they want to keep and some that they would eliminate. I would like to know what specific ones the NDP would like to eliminate.
Second, is the NDP proposing in its tax reform proposals, tax reform that would have a neutral tax impact effect so that personal income taxes might go down and corporate taxes would go up, or would there only be a rise in corporate taxes?
Finally, if the New Democratic Party is proposing some sort of neutral tax impact or a reduction in personal income taxes, how does it propose to raise the money to pay for all the increased expenditures which the Hon. Member proposes in his speech?

subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member's questions are certainly valid. I am delighted to hear that the Hon. Member for York East (Mr. Redway) is an avid reader of the various reports of Tax Probe 86. I promise to send him a copy of the next report which will come out shortly. In fact, by the end of the year or early in 1987, we will have consulted further and will have more feedback in terms of our findings so far. At that point we intend to come to conclusions in terms of some of the questions the Hon. Member raises.
For example, in our most recent report on corporation tax, we indicated that there is a solid case for certain tax concessions, or tax expenditures, to small and medium-sized businesses. Currently they are paying a net rate which is higher than that of big businesses, rather than the other way around. That, to us, seems to be a perverse situation, particularly when so much job creation has come from small and medium-sized businesses.
The Hon. Member certainly reports my Leader accurately and, as so often has happened, I think my Leader may have been a prophet before his time by a few months. Since January, 1986, there has been no further job creation in the Canadian economy. The 500,000 jobs that the Government talks about were in 1984 and 1985. The trend has not continued. I certainly do not find a rate of unemployment of 9.7 per cent acceptable. Perhaps the Government finds that acceptable.
I suspect that most of the improvement that we saw in approximately the first year under the Government was a result of growth that had spilled over from the American economy. Now that that economy has turned the other way, there is no buoyancy from the Government. In fact, the taxes which have been levied on ordinary Canadians are having the effect of depressing the economy. Therefore, when we spoke of hundreds of thousands of jobs that would be affected, they are the jobs that should have been created by a dynamic economy in 1986. They are the jobs which would have put teenagers in Chicoutimi and Newfoundland back to work and would have given women opportunities to re-enter the labour force in
October 9, 1986

Vancouver. However, those people do not have those opportunities because of the drag on the economy by the Government's tax policies.
The Hon. Member asks whether or not tax reform should be neutral. 1 am surprised to hear him suggest that the Government may even slip away from its commitment in the Throne Speech to reduce the rates of personal income tax. He is suggesting that that is a wrong move. I beleive that personal income taxes for many working Canadians are too high. In order to have a fair tax system we must bring those tax rates down at the same time that we increase the share that is taken by the corporate sector. We should not try to bootleg another personal tax by calling it a business transfer tax.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Debate. The Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion and Canada Post (Mr. Cote).

speakeroldname: Hon. Michel Cote (Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion and Canada Post):
speakerposition: Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion; Minister responsible for Canada Post Corporation
subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 am very pleased today to take part in the debate on the Address in reply to the Speech from the Throne.
I am all the more pleased to do so that the Speech from the Throne advocates a number of initiatives which have become essential to most Canadians, particularly those who have to deal with business circles, be they owners, investors or working men and women.
Mr. Speaker, like my hon. colleagues, Canadians are quite aware that our country is now experiencing unstable economic conditions to which it must constantly seek to adapt.
Ours is an industrial and trading nation. We depend on trade, be it to develop our raw materials or to maintain the economic strength of our industries and our service sector. Canadians are first-rate managers, innovators and traders. Our labour force is skilled and very productive and, more important still, our competitiveness is second to none in practically all economic sectors, despite our own limited domestic markets.
Most international experts agree that we do have such qualities. In his speech last Friday the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) referred to the European Management Forum. What are those experts telling us? They are telling us that Canada's competitiveness has improved to such an extent over the last two years that, on the basis of their own classification, Canada climbed from 11th to 6th among the major industrial nations. Not a bad performance compared with that of our competitors. If we persevere, Mr. Speaker, I can assure you that we can do even better. However, we have to face three major challenges.
First, as a trading nation, we must have full access to the international markets and capital necessary for our economic growth. Our welfare depends on it. In addition, as a greatly industrialized country, we must continue to be productive and competitive internationally. We must keep up with the latest technology and use all our creativity and ingenuity to adapt to
The Address-Mr. Cote
the evolution of the world economy. The economic future of our country requires us to do so.
Finally, as a nation made up of different geographic and cultural elements and based on the principles of equity and solidarity, we must try to achieve a balanced growth in all regions of the country. This is necessary for the integrity of our Confederation.
You, Mr. Speaker, and all Hon. Members know that economic renewal has been this Government's first priority. We have achieved real and substantial progress since September, 1984, but do not take my word for it. Let me quote as follows from the annual report of The Canadian Manufacturers' Association as it commented on the economic accomplishment of this administration:
The restrictions of FIR A, reflecting a narrow and destructive nationalism, were removed and Investment Canada is now working aggressively to encourage investment here ... The previous acrimony in federal-provincial relations has given way to a more positive nation-building approach to our problems.
The past year saw continued progress in restoring fiscal sanity in federal Government finances ...
A competition Bill was ... introduced which ... contains explicit recognition of international competition while at the same time providing... protection against abuse of dominant position ...
Major tax changes aimed at greater neutrality . .. were also introduced.
This is a most impressive record, one that is certainly the envy of some of my hon. friends who used to sit on this side of the House. Naturally, Mr. Laurent Thibault, the President of The Canadian Manufacturers' Association, gives his Members credit for assisting in these accomplishments. I most certainly concur, and I am sure all Hon. Members would agree with me that all Canadians should take credit for this record, as well as for continued low inflation, lower interest rates and lower unemployment.
Obviously, as Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion I am particularly concerned with reconciling the imperatives of industrial competitiveness with balanced economic opportunities across Canada. My Department is dedicated to the development of Canadian industry, especially in the manufacturing and service sectors, and to building on the opportunities for development that exist across Canada. We intend to achieve these objectives in co-operation with the private sector and with the provincial Governments.
As Minister responsible for Investment Canada I am also concerned that Canada obtain a growing share of international investment because we need this investment to increase employment in all parts of the country.

Mr. Speaker, one of the crucial contributing causes to slow development is often a lack of capital, and in this regard, I would like to remind the House that the first Bill we introduced in this place was the one which created Investment Canada. This agency, for which I have the honour to be

October 9, 1986
The Address-Mr. Cote
responsible, immediately proved itself to be a major tool in promoting both Canadian and foreign investments in this country.
Thus, the Government was able to ensure the free inflow of the capital required to develop the many resources of our country and see that they are used for the economic renewal of all our regions. As you know, a major part of the Speech from the Throne deals with this issue of industrial and regional development. If I may, Mr. Speaker, I would like to discuss this subject further. Regional development remains one of our main priorities. Economic and social conditions have obviously improved throughout Canada in the last two years. Economic renewal continues and our social policy is already having noticeable results. However, as a Government committed to eliminate regional disparities, we must unfortunately recognize that, in spite of decades of efforts and billions of dollars, there are still gross employment and income inequities in certain regions. The Government therefore intends to make a renewed and firm commitment that each region in the country must achieve its full potential.
As mentioned by the Prime Minister in the Throne Speech, the Government intends to reassess a number of programs related to regional development. We are convinced that this evaluation should be made with three very clear and specific principles in mind.
First, we believe that regional development must come from the potential and the people of each region. Experience has shown that, with appropriate assistance, Canadians have the will, the determination and the ability to stimulate the development of their regional economies.
Second, our economic development programs and the administration and provision of our services to businesses must be much more decentralized than they are now.
Third, our decision-making and benefit-paying mechanisms should be much more efficient, faster and more sensitive to the users' interests.
A review of our regional development programs will continue in co-operation with provincial governments. As Hon. Members in this House are aware, consultations will resume at the highest level on October 17 in Charlottetown, when the Prime Minister meets with the Premiers of the Atlantic Provinces.
Mr. Speaker, much has already been done through the federal-provincial committee of Ministers in charge of Regional Economic Development. I would like to indicate that the committee already has met six times since February 1985. A committee of officials will be submitting a report to us later this year, and its recommendations should help us implement our commitment to prevent wasting even one single dollar in that vital effort for Canada.

As you know from the Speech from the Throne, Mr. Speaker, the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency will be
established without undue delay, bearing in mind the need to consult with provincial Governments and the region's business and community leaders. The mandate and organization of the agency will reflect the three principles I have already described, that is, development based on human resources and opportunities in the Atlantic Provinces, with decentralized decision-making and better delivery.
I emphasize that these principles will guide our efforts, not only in Atlantic Canada but in all parts of Canada as well, particularly in western Canada where special emphasis will be given to diversifying the region's economic base. This will clearly confirm the Government's commitment to balanced economic growth in every part of this beautiful country. Just as Canada cannot afford to neglect the important contribution all regions make to the national good, neither can we afford to have half our population performing at less than its full potential.
Women, in particular, suffer from the inequities built into our society. They are doubly disadvantaged if economic difficulties in their region adversely affect their employment potential and the quality of their family lives.
As this Government seeks to address regional disparity, women will undoubtedly provide important guidance about the right approaches and the much needed policy initiatives. It is my hope that they will enjoy more and better employment and personal opportunities as their communities are revitalized. Women will be part of the new partnership formed between the federal Government and Canada's regions. It is my belief that they will share equally in the prosperity and the stability that will be the result.
However, this is only one side of the equation. We are vitally committed to enhancing the development of industry everywhere in Canada. With this in mind, we intend to re-examine our main industrial support program, the Industrial Regional Development Program, or IRDP.
This program was introduced by the previous Government to meet a multiplicity of objectives, perhaps too many objectives. The complexity of the program and the differential treatment of some areas has meant, among other things, that the Government has not been able to support a number of quality projects, particularly in western Canada. We intend to look very closely at the effectiveness of the existing tier system that determines the level of support that can be provided to projects in various regions.

Mr. Speaker, in the course of that review of the RIDP, we will also consider the various possible ways of responding to one of the basic concerns of this Government, that is productivity.
The search for productivity is essential to allow and ensure the development of new manufacturing processes and also to
October 9, 1986

make possible the marketing of new goods and services. In our view, invention and technology transfer must go hand in hand.
History shows the best borrowers or adapters of technology often are those already involved in research and development. We must therefore have a much more balanced approach. We cannot do everything ourselves, but we can neither be content with borrowing technology from others.
The private sector all across Canada has show leadership in the area of innovation and technology. Northern Telecom, for instance, has been marketing Canadian communication technology throughout the world for a number of years.

Alcan is the largest and probably one of the most efficient aluminium producers in the world based on its past research efforts. It is now becoming a world leader in the development of new materials. Such companies as National Sea Products, Fishery Products International and Canada Packers are using innovation and new technologies to diversify and improve their products and productivity.
In addition, there are hundreds of new companies across Canada, such as Process Technology in New Brunswick, Ogivar Inc. in Quebec, Diffracto in Windsor, SED in Saskatchewan, to name only a few, that are achieving remarkable results in international high technolgy.
For Canada, continued research and development and the ability to import technologies, to apply and build upon them and to market the results will be key elements of an improved competitive position. We require investment capital and linkages with world industry to accomplish this objective.
Our Government established Investment Canada as a national focal point to encourage the essential investment and creative partnerships necessary to this critical priority.

For instance, last year the Agency was involved with the Province of Alberta and the Independent Petroleum Association in a series of investment promotion seminars throughout Europe and the United States.
More recently, officials from Investment Canada also joined with representatives of the Ontario Government in a trip to Japan.
Moreover, Investment Canada is also involved on behalf of the Canadian Government in a number of other activities, such as consulting with national and international trade groups and also international promotion missions.
That work must go on, Mr. Speaker, and this Government's commitment to encourage investment in all its forms is vitally important.

During the coming year, Investment Canada will focus on contributing to the improvement of our technological infrastructure to promote and attract technology-bearing investment
The Address-Mr. Cote
in Canada; working with Canadian business to promote a more global orientation; and seeking new forms of investments, such as strategic alliances among Canadian and international firms.

Mr. Speaker, the Government is determined to review and update, if necessary, its regional and industrial development support programs to make sure that all parts of the country are treated equitably and that the Canadian industry continues to improve its international competitiveness.
However, the funds allocated to regional and industrial development are nothing but a few drops in the ocean of the Canadian economy. Our programs, therefore, have to be very selective, which means that investments generally should be made without any State intervention.
That is why we want the private sector to become the engine of our economic growth. In fact, the Government has made every effort to lift obstacles by encouraging deregulation and creating a climate favourable to business endeavours.

The business sector needs a Government that will provide a productive and competitive environment, that will provide support as required and that will stay the course in the development process. We are that Government, and we have that commitment. We can develop as partners.

subsubtopic: RESULTS OF GALLUP POLL
speechtext:
This is a great day, Mr. Speaker, because this morning's newspapers reported on a Gallup poll clearly showing that the Progressive Conservative Government is in a free fall and the Liberal Party on the rise.
It is also a great day because, in a few minutes, Hon. Members will be extending a warm welcome to the successful candidate in the Saint-Maurice election, our colleague Mr. Grondin. Mr. Speaker, I should think that the Progressive Conservative Government and the Right Hon. the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) are getting a very clear message: Canadians generally and Quebecers in particular can hardly wait to turf the Conservative gang right out.

Mr. Speaker, this week's resignation of the Director of Finance in the Manitoba region of the Department of Indian Affairs has lifted the lid a little higher on the unholy administrative mess which exists in that Department.
Let it be known by all Hon. Members that in many areas- education, child welfare, and local government-the Indian people of Manitoba have led the way in self-government. However, at every turn they are frustrated by a Department which will not let go and wants to continue controlling, dominating, and monitoring them. Even more serious, funds appropriated by Parliament for Indian people do not get to them in the way in which we in the House intend.
An inefficient, maladministered Department soaks up a huge portion of these funds and directs them at will, in open defiance of Parliament and of the Minister himself. It is our task as Members of Parliament to reveal these facts and to demand a new relationship between the Government of Canada and the Indian people of the country.

subtopic: ELECTION CAMPAIGN VOLUNTEERS-PROHIBITION ON ACCESS TO MILITARY BASES
ELECTION CAMPAIGN VOLUNTEERS-PROHIBITION ON ACCESS TO MILITARY BASES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a shame that the new Minister of National Defence (Mr. Beatty) is continuing his Government's policy of making Armed Forces personnel and their families into second-class citizens. In this case, volunteers in provincial election campaigns are being forbidden to set foot on military bases. This is ridiculous.
People living on bases are affected by provincial government actions. They have the right to elect a provincial Government of their choice. They should be allowed to receive information so that they can make an informed, intelligent choice on election day.
No one is urging the Armed Forces to take part in some sinister plot. Political Parties are merely urging people on military bases to exercise their basic constitutional right to make a choice in a democratic election. Even the former Associate Minister of National Defence could not justify keeping candidates off military bases. He admitted: "It's hard to come up with a reason why you wouldn't allow that on military bases in this day and age".
October 9, 1986

subtopic: SITUATION OF INDUSTRY-CALL FOR GOVERNMENT ASSISTANCE
SITUATION OF INDUSTRY-CALL FOR GOVERNMENT ASSISTANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise today on a matter of utmost urgency concerning the state of crisis which exists in the shipbuilding industry. Since the Conservative Government was elected, every meaningful federal assistance program to the industry has been curtailed. Essentially the former Minister of Transport said "Don't expect us to help you", and thousands of shipyard workers across the country have been thrown out of work.
This kind of government inaction is simply unacceptable to Canadians. The Government, especially the Minister of Transport (Mr. Crosbie) and the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion (Mr. Cote), must take immediate action to assist the Canadian shipbuilding industry. The Ministers should take every step to encourage domestic demand for shipping capacity and to see to it that this demand is met by Canadian shipyards, not by subsidized yards in other countries.
For too long the Government has said that this is a worldwide problem which cannot be solved, and then washed its hands. Canadians expect their Government to take positive action in the face of adversity, not simply to run away and hide. Canadians feel that it is high time that the Government and the Minister of Transport and the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion live up to their responsibilities-

subtopic: SITUATION OF INDUSTRY-CALL FOR GOVERNMENT ASSISTANCE

subtopic: ANNIVERSARY OF ELECTION OF FIRST CANADIAN PARLIAMENTARIAN OF UKRAINIAN ORIGIN
ANNIVERSARY OF ELECTION OF FIRST CANADIAN PARLIAMENTARIAN OF UKRAINIAN ORIGIN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I attended the sixtieth anniversary celebration of the election of Michael Luchkovich to the House of Commons, the first Canadian parliamentarian of Ukrainian origin. Throughout his nine years of service in the House of Commons he demonstrated that no problem was too great, that a fair and just solution could always be found. He was highly respected by all Members and made an indelible and most favourable impression on the Government of the day.
He was a well-tempered statesman, a man of courage. Without his translations of Ukrainian literature into English, especially of Ukrainian pioneer life in western Canada, we Canadians would be missing an integral part of our national history.
As we note this special anniversary, we should recall Michael Luchkovich's firm commitment that "true
patriotism... includes persistence and frugality even under trying circumstances".

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased that Canada Post is currently re-evaluating its previously announced closure of the Norwood Grove post office in order to seek a better alternative.
On June 12 and again on July 10 of this year, I was assured by the Corporation that no such closing was being contemplated. At the exact same time managers were negotiating with the union the changes necessary to effect the closing. The last two evenings the corporation has met with a few selected constituents in a "by invitation" only meeting to consult. Although we appreciate this consultation, Mr. Speaker, my constituents and I would be more impressed with truly public consultation.
[DOT] (MIO)
Canadians deserve good postal service at a reasonable cost, not slick PR, shoddy management and intractable collective agreements.

Mr. Speaker, the service to my Norwood electors must be maintained.

Mr. Speaker, for years the Indian people of Canada have been telling us that they have been mistreated by the Indian Affairs Department. For years people in Parliament were skeptical about what Indian people were telling Canadians. However, the recent revelations by the Department in Winnipeg which follow the Curry audit indicates that what the Indian people have been telling us is true.
The Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. McKnight) has indicated that he is willing to have an R.C.M.P. investigation into whether or not Indian Affairs was acting in a legal manner. That, surely, is not the right answer, Mr. Speaker. What is missing at the present time is the relationship of trust which historically has been between the federal Government and the Indian people. That has been utterly destroyed by the various departmental officials over the last number of years and by the inaction of various Ministers

October 9, 1986
of Indian Affairs. What we need is a completely independent check into all the actions and decision-making processes of Indian Affairs and, if that is not done, the trust will never be re-established.

[ Translation]

maintopic: THE LATE FRANQOISE GAUDET-SMET COMMEMORATIVE STAMP ISSUE ADVOCATED
THE LATE FRANQOISE GAUDET-SMET COMMEMORATIVE STAMP ISSUE ADVOCATED
speechtext:
Last September 4, Mr. Speaker, the people of the riding of Lotbiniere and all other Quebecers were saddened to hear of the death of Mrs. Franfoise Gaudet-Smet, an outstanding Quebecer. Mrs. Gaudet-Smet was a pioneer in her field, an irreplaceable personality whose authenticity, warmth, colourful verve and boundless hospitality will remain forever present in our minds. Mr. Speaker, many of her friends were amazed at her vitality and working energy, but especially at her ever probing mind full of ideas and projects.
This is why I would urge the Minister responsible for Canada Post to issue a commemorative stamp in her honour. To support this request, Mr. Speaker, suffice it to mention that Mrs. Gaudet-Smet was awarded the Order of Canada, the Order of Quebec, the Bene Merenti Medal, the Gold Medal of the Governor General, the Literary Prize of the Societe Saint-Jean-Baptiste, and the Ordre de la fidelite franqaise.

subtopic: JAPANESE-CANADIANS INTERNED DURING WORLD WAR II

speechtext:
Mr. Sergio March! (York West): Mr. Speaker, the new Minister of State for Multiculturalism (Mr. Crombie) has a number of important priorities which he must urgently address. Near the top of that agenda is the issue of Japanese-Canadian redress. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) committed himself and his Government to two essential ingredients: establishing a negotiating process and conducting these talks with and through the National Association of Japanese Canadians. Unfortunately the two former Ministers failed to honour either of these two crucial promises and thus sowed the seeds of mistrust and non-confidence within the Japanese-Canadian community.
Today that same community, Canadians, and this Parliament remain hopeful that the third Minister to tackle this issue in two years will honour the previous commitments and initiate meaningful discussions within a well defined and ongoing structure as soon as possible.
It is high time that the Conservative Government ends the delay and the rhetoric and resolves this matter with the dignity that it rightfully deserves.

maintopic: JOB CREATION POTENTIAL OF PETROLEUM INDUSTRY
JOB CREATION POTENTIAL OF PETROLEUM INDUSTRY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in March of this year I reported to the House that 650,000 Canadians from coast to coast were dependent upon Canada's petroleum industry for their livelihood. Today that figure has dropped to 600,000 with a further anticipated loss of 20,000 jobs. That represents 70,000 people. These are the sad consequences of the present crisis in the industry brought about by the drastic drop in world crude prices.
It is important to know that of every dollar spent by the petroleum industry for machinery and equipment, 42 cents is spent in Ontario, 29 cents in Alberta, 13 cents in Quebec, and the remaining 16 cents in other regions of Canada. This is the contribution that a healthy industry can make for the benefit of all Canada. Two jobs in Canada's petroleum industry create three jobs in other parts of Canada, primarily Ontario and Quebec. The energy industry is job creative.

Mr. Speaker, today's Globe and Mail reports that the Conservative caucus committee has written to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) urging that ministerial permits for potential immigrants already in Canada be issued only by the Minister's office "rather than allowing politically non-aligned bureaucrats free rein with 90 per cent of them". What an outrageous demand. What a perversion of justice towards refugees and relatives of Canadians deserving humane treatment. Thousands of refugees and others are awaiting processing of their applications and deserve Minister's permits. To deny permits to some because they might not vote Tory would be shameful.
I regret that the Hon. Member for Parkdale-High Park (Mr. Witer), my colleague on the Standing Committee on Labour, Employment and Immigration, is named in this story as chairman. I call upon him to return to this House and either assure us that he had no part whatever in the proposal reported today by The Globe and Mail, or else announce his resignation from that committee.
October 9, 1986

subtopic: CALL FOR INCLUSION OF PROPERTY RIGHTS
CALL FOR INCLUSION OF PROPERTY RIGHTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is Private Property Week in Canada. The right to own property is part of the Canadian heritage. Many people came to this country because they wanted to own land, own a home, or own a farm. Why then is it the only fundamental freedom not protected in the Canadian Constitution?
You know what? In 1981, for 48 hours, it was in our Charter of Rights, but during the weekend the Liberals caved into demands of the NDP and took it out, to the shame of both the Liberals and the NDP. Of course, nationalization will be more difficult when the right to own property is enshrined in the Constitution, but only the communists and the socialists are interested in nationalization anyway.
The Canadian Real Estate Association, the Canadian Bar Association, and the Canadian Chamber of Commerce, along with most Canadians, want to see the right to own property placed in our Constitution. So let's get to it and put it in.

Mr. Speaker, this summer Atlantic Canadians found out just how well their interests are being represented in the federal Cabinet. The senior Minister from the region said Atlantic Canadians should stop griping about unemployment and consider instead the plight of those living in Haiti or Bangladesh. Our standards are too high, he said, if we use southern Ontario as our yardstick.
I have never heard such marlarkey. What nonsense! The Minister's comments are a kick in the teeth to struggling Atlantic Canadians. They are proof of the Government's lack of concern for those living in the Atlantic region, the unemployed, the fishemen, and the farmers. We do not need to be reminded that we are a thousand times better off and luckier than those living in Haiti or Bangladesh. We need Ministers committed to regional development, Ministers who will make a difference. It is now quite clear that Atlantic Canadians will have to wait for a change in Government before the issue of regional disparity is given serious attention.

subtopic: CANADIAN RURAL TRANSITION PROGRAM-RETRAINING OPPORTUNITIES FOR FARMERS
CANADIAN RURAL TRANSITION PROGRAM-RETRAINING OPPORTUNITIES FOR FARMERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Canadian Rural Transition Program is being welcomed by those members of the farm community who understand its purpose. In some constituencies as many as 70 people have applied for the program. No one wants to see farmers leave their way of life but many are faced with a difficult decision and need financial assistance to be able to make choices about their future. Until now, farmers have been denied the relocation and retraining opportunities available to the non-farm community.
An urbanite who loses his or her job can go on unemployment insurance, take a training course through Manpower, or get a student loan and return to school. Until now farmers were not eligible for any of these programs. That was an injustice, and I am pleased to see that this federal Government has addressed this inequity at long last. The program gives many farmers facing severe financial difficulty the opportunity to make choices about their future, an opportunity they have long deserved.

subtopic: CALL FOR RESUMPTION OF RECORD KEEPING BY STATISTICS CANADA
CALL FOR RESUMPTION OF RECORD KEEPING BY STATISTICS CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first it was cancellation of the census, and now an attempt by Statistics Canada to eliminate abortion statistics. StatsCan has once again been the victim of a savage and vicious attack by the Tory Government. Now that I have congratulated six Conservative Members, which for me is a great deal, I would like to express an opinion I think is shared by Canadians in general, namely that in this Speech from the Throne, the Progressive Conservative Government has been a great disappointment. After all, when the Government decided to prorogue and delay resumption of

We thought the Government would take this opportunity to make a fresh start and come in with new ideas and new ways of doing things. Above all, Canadians were expecting some leadership from this Government. Unfortunately, Canadians who were counting on seeing some original ideas in the Speech from the Throne and some new and concrete solutions to the real problems Canada is facing today, all these people were terribly disappointed, because this Speech from the Throne is the very essence of platitude. We have been presented with a document that lacks any imagination whatsoever. It reflects the image of a Government that has exhausted its energy after barely two years in power.
This Government is already forced to rehash the promises made during the last election campaign and in its first Speech from the Throne. Mr. Speaker, it is obvious that this Government, after asking Canadians to support its plan to clean up our public finances and reduce the deficit, has done the exact opposite. And it is abundantly clear that the first prize for deficits in this country goes to the present Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson).
This Government got elected by promising jobs, jobs, jobs. You will recall, Mr. Speaker, that during the election campaign, the present Prime Minister said: We have only three priorities: jobs, jobs, jobs.

Again the Government has failed in its objective. Again it is clear that the Government is trying to portray a situation which is not accurate.
I would like to quote from an article written in the Toronto Star by David Crane, a writer on political and economic affairs. He said:
The latest unemployment figures suggest that luck has run out for Prime Minister Brian Mulroney and his cabinet colleagues. They can no longer count on continued recovery from the 1981-8? recession to fulfil their campaign promises of "jobs, jobs, jobs''.
Now they will have to come up with new approaches of their own if further progress is to be made in the fight against unemployment.

October 9, 1986
The Address-Mr. Ouellet .
The fact is, Mr. Speaker, that the Conservative Government, which promised to find jobs for Canadians, is today faced with a situation where more than one million Canadian workers are jobless. It is a fact that this Government, which promised to find jobs for the people of this country, has failed to live up to the expectations of Canadians, and that across this country, there are still far too many men and women, and especially young men and women, who are out of work. And the platitudes in a Speech from the Throne that has failed to announce any concrete measures for creating jobs in Canada are certainly not going to solve the problem. Acutally, the new Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Bouchard) unwittingly gave a clear indication of the bleak realities Canadians have to contend with, in his answer to my colleague, the Hon. Member for Shefford (Mr. Lapierre), who was upset that the Prime Minister gave orders to have a penitentiary, that would normally have been built in the riding of Drummond built in his own riding, at an additional cost to the Canadian taxpayer of several million dollars.
In fact, early this week, my hon. friend from Shefford put his question to the Member who normally should have answered the question, but the Minister of Employment and Immigration rose instead and said the following: We must realize that 38 per cent of the people in the Prime Minister's (Mr. Mulroney) riding receive part of their income from unemployment insurance or are on welfare.
So the Minister of Employment and Immigration agrees with what we have been saying for many months, which is that many people are not included in the unemployment statistics, since the figure for the Prime Minister's riding is about 15 per cent.
So what is being used as an excuse for the Prime Minister's decision to have the penitentiary built in his riding is the fact that 38 per cent of the people in that riding are receiving some form of government aid or are no longer considered as being on the labour market because they have ceased to report to the manpower centres to look for work, probably because they are convinced there are no jobs available anyway.
This situation, as reflected in the 38 per cent figure, probably reflects the true state of our Canadian economy. Not 10 per cent or 11 per cent of Canadians are in difficulty and qualify as being unemployed, but 35 per cent or 38 or 40 per cent of Canadians are in difficulty, are unemployed or are convinced that they won't be able to find employment. The Conservative Government promised them jobs and now, two years later, they are living in poverty, and they are so depressed they are not even looking for work because no jobs are available.
Mr. Speaker, the situation is shocking and intolerable, and the fact that the Minister of Employment and Immigration is wasting his time trying to justify an intolerably partisan
decision on the part of the Prime Minister is certainly not to his credit.
I have to say that the Minister of Employment and Immigration probably felt that he had to rush to the defence of his Prime Minister, but by doing so he revealed the real condition of the Canadian economy.
Roughly 10 per cent of Canadians are unemployed, another 10 per cent are on social welfare, and yet another 10 per cent or more have completely given up looking for employment because they are convinced there are no jobs available.
Well, the fancy rhetoric of the Prime Minister is no longer good enough. People want action now and expect this Government to come up with concrete and specific programs to spur the economy.
I would suggest that the most tragic mistake of this Government has been to imagine that it had to start from scratch in every field. Here is a telling example: the Minister of Transport (Mr. Crosbie) who found the VIA Rail file on his desk. The previous Government had launched a five-year action plan to set the Crown corporation VIA Rail back on the right track, according to a well-balanced and rational process. Well now, instead of accepting this action plan under which, first, certain underused and non-profitable lines would have been dropped, second, adequate rolling stock would have been bought and, third, the administration would have been revamped, this Government, this new Minister threw everything overboard and went back to square one so that now, two years later, VIA Rail has not progressed one inch. It does not even have a single locomotive nor a single new railway car to give better service to the traveling public.
That is an example of a Government which is unable to make decisions. It appointed a committee chaired by Mr. Horner to review the whole question. The report was handed to the Minister of Transport six months ago and the Government has not done anything about it yet. In other words, ever since the Conservatives were elected to office we got nothing but more studies and more consultations, and this Government has yet to make one significant and specific decision.
I conclude my remarks by saying that this Throne Speech is the most disappointing thing we have seen in a long time. Unfortunately, Canadians have a Government that is marking time, that takes one step forward and two steps backwards, that does not know how to manage public affairs, that does not know how to administer the affairs of the state. Earlier in its mandate, we could accept inexperienced Ministers making blunders, but two years later, the Government can no longer hide behind the screen of political inexperience. This Government must have the courage to take the important decisions that are needed to solve the problem of unemployment in Canada. We need only look at the Throne Speech to see that, unfortunately, this Government does not have that political courage, and I am not surprised to see that showing how much Canadians are disappointed with this Government.
October 9, 1986

I am very much heartened by the appearance in this House today of our new colleague, the Hon. Member for Saint-Maurice (Mr. Grondin) who is joining all those who will go on fighting this inefficient Government and the inappropriate decisions it is taking on behalf of the Canadian people.
