speakeroldname: Hon. Pat Carney (Minister for International Trade):
subsubtopic: RESUMPTION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Canadian trade policy must reflect a basic fact of Canadian economic life-our small population. A small domestic market means that secure access to foreign markets is critical. In Canada, trade means jobs. Some 27 per cent of our GNP is directly related to exports. One in three Canadian jobs depends, in some form, upon trade. Unlike countries with large domestic markets, such as the U.S., Japan or Brazil, our industries require markets larger than our own to achieve efficient economies of scale and specialization. Our companies need access to those markets to justify investment in modern plants and equipment and expensive research and development.
However, secure access to foreign markets is important for more than just export-oriented companies. It is also important for Canadian consumers and our retail business sector. If our companies are not internationally competitive, they will not be competitive at home. That would mean higher costs to Canadian consumers and less disposable income for consumer and business spending. And that means fewer jobs and less economic activity in our country. These are the basic facts of Canadian economic life, and they cannot be wished away. It is for these reasons that from the time of the Great Depression successive Governments have sought trade liberalization through international negotiations.
The expansion of the world trading system has brought great benefits to Canada. Our exporting ability has given us a standard of living that is the envy of most countries of the world. It has provided us with the wealth to develop accessible health care, affordable education, equalization policies, income security programs and national cultural institutions-all the institutions and values which really define the Canadian way of life.
Pragmatism and realism have led us to initiate a two-track trade policy made up of bilateral one-on-one negotiations with the United States, by far our most important customer, reinforced by multilateral negotiations under the auspices of the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade. I would like to review some of the realities behind this two-track approach.
In the 40 years since the formation of the GATT, the international trading system has changed. Four events stand out. First, there was the formation of the European Economic Community and many other small regional trading blocks, such as the ASEAN block, the Australia-New Zealand pact and the European Free Trade Association. Second, there was the dramatic rise of Japan as a major economic power. Third, there was the emergence of certain newly industrialized nations such as South Korea and Brazil. The fourth event was the proliferation of independent nation states resulting from post-war decolonization.
These events have changed the international environment. In today's world there are many more competitors producing the goods that we produce. Moreover, the emergence of regional trading arrangements means that some of our traditional markets are not as open to us as they once were. In short, competition in world markets is increasing. A Canadian trade
The Address-Miss Carney
policy that seeks to safeguard our interests must reflect these realities.
These fundamental changes in the world economy have been reflected in the GATT. The GATT has evolved from a small club of like-minded countries into a much more complex group of countries having vastly different competitive strengths and trading interests. This has led to more complicated and lengthy multilateral trade negotiations. For instance, the last round, the Tokyo Round, lasted from 1973 to 1979.
Canada is a uniquely important player in this coalition of countries. We are a bridge between the less-developed countries and the economic super-powers. Our interests are allied with other resource-based producers. This was demonstrated by the pivotal role that Canada played by putting agriculture on the agenda of the GATT negotiations at Punta del Este, Uruguay. At the same time we have common interests with the largest trading nations. We are a member of the Quadrilateral, the informal group of the largest traders in the world, along with the United States, Japan and the European Community. We met at Sintra, Portugual just prior to the GATT in Uruguay. We played an active role in coordinating our positions for the GATT negotiations. So there should be no doubts that we are an important member of the multilateral trading community. There should be no mistaking this Government's commitment to the GATT. We are an active, dynamic and leading player in the GATT. We are absolutely committed to the General Agreement and to the Uruguay Round.
However, in reaffirming our commitment to the GATT we must realize that it alone cannot protect all our interests. The vast majority of our exports go to one national market, that is, the U.S. market, which now takes 78 per cent of all our exports. So we are engaged in bilateral negotiations with the United States for only one reason-it is in Canada's interest to do so.
What do we seek to achieve? We want to redefine the rules that presently govern trade between our two countries. We want to secure and to enhance our access to U.S. markets. We want to lock those rules and that security of access into the form of a long-term binding treaty between both countries.
Let me first discuss secure access. There is a thicket of trade laws in the U.S. at the disposal of any interest group that wants to bring an action against Canada. Since 1980, well over 500 complaints have been brought forward in the U.S. These cases have become increasingly complex and have spawned an unprecedented number of appeals. The proliferation of trade complaints in the past five years has caused grave concern to Canada. These cases complicate investment decisions, because to be successful Canadian producers need security of access to foreign markets.
If the rules keep changing, then that security is jeopardized and diminished. However, what is equally important is a disturbing reluctance in the U.S. to accept the verdict when U.S. interests do not win a case. We see that in the softwood
254

October 9, 1986
The Address-Miss Carney
lumber case. We won the case in 1983. We then faced a number of legislative initiatives seeking in one way or other to limit our exports to the U.S. We then faced a fact-finding investigation and yet another countervail action this year. Now, the threat is that if the U.S. industry does not get what it wants there will be the likelihood of more Congressional action. This is why we seek new rules. We seek a better shield against the forces of protectionism. The existing rules may be law, but their enforcement does not always lead to justice. We want more certainty. We want a more confident environment for investors and producers in Canada. This, in turn, will generate jobs and economic growth.
What about enhanced access? One example is our industries' ability to sell goods to the U.S. state and federal Governments. For example, the "Buy American requirement prohibits the use of foreign steel in projects funded under certain acts. This closes an important part of the U.S. market to our producers. We want better access to these markets so that our world-class technology in areas such as telecommunications and electrical generating equipment can compete on an equal footing with U.S. producers.
There are many other trade actions taken by the U.S. which irritate us. 1 am reminded of the Prime Minister's words that we are best friends, America and Canada, and that we are each other's biggest trading partners, but at times it is difficult to be friendly with your best friend. I could also mention, for instance, potash, uranium, the wheat subsidy war and other U.S. support practices.
However, we are not walking away. Rather, we are seeking through negotiations a better framework for trade between us.
The U.S. administration, for its part, has indicated that it sees important benefits for its country. Canada is the largest market for U.S. exports and it is one of the few markets in which U.S. exports are increasing. Canada is the largest recipient of direct U.S. investment and millions of cross-border transactions link our two national economies.
The U.S., of course, has its concerns and we are willing to listen to them. We will adjust for them where we are able to do so. That is the process of negotiation. Any trade treaty clearly must be beneficial to both partners.
Some who oppose this initiative say we are undermining the GATT by advancing our interest on a bilateral basis. That is simply wrong. A bilateral agreement is consistent with GATT rules. Moreover, our bilateral talks with the U.S. are not only consistent with the GATT but could serve as multilateral models. We are well aware that Canada-U.S. agreements in such areas as procurement and services could be models for multilateral action. We are negotiating with this in mind.
So those are some of the realities that have prompted us to embark upon this two-track approach. They make a compelling case for our two-track policy. The critics who are here today have a responsibility to address these same realities and
to tell Canadians how their policies meet the needs of Canadians today. I suspect they will not be able to because their policies are not based on fact or supported by past experience and their policies do not meet the needs of Canada in today's world.
I recognize that much of this criticism has been directed at the hearts of Canadians, not their heads. Canadians have been warned of the traumatic adjustments that will flow from an arrangement and they have been warned that our cultural sovereignty is at stake. Those are two false accusations, so let me take a minute to address these two fears.
First, regarding the trauma of change, let us just put this in perspective. Canada has been reducing its trade barriers step by step since the beginning of GATT in 1947. Canadians have not only survived this process but have prospered under it. If Canadians have prospered through seven rounds of trade liberalization, why would the next step be any different?
Second, there is the issue of cultural sovereignty. I would like to remind the House that there were two important events in the life of Canada which took place in the late 1940s. One was the creation of the GATT, the start of the trade liberalization process that has continued to this day. The other was the Massey Royal Commission on the National Development of the Arts, Letters and Sciences, the start of a cultural development process that has also continued to this day. These two processes went hand in hand because it was the prosperity created by trade liberalization that allowed us to create all those institutions and programs which helped to define us as Canadians today.
Just as trade liberalization continues, the challenge to build a national identity continues today. We in the Government recognize that and we have said very clearly to our negotiators that this Government's ability to protect and enhance Canadian culture is non-negotiable. We want a country whose people can communicate with one another through the arts and the popular media. The essence which makes us Canadian cannot and will not be compromised.
Before I close my remarks, let me make a final point, Mr. Speaker. So far, I have talked about our two-track trade policy. Let me note another element of our over-all trade strategy, the need to seek new export opportunities. I view the promotion of Canadian exports as being a key element of my portfolio. Essential as it may be, it is not enough to negotiate changes in the rules governing trade. We must continue to seek new markets for our goods and services. As was stated in the Speech from the Throne, particular emphasis will be placed upon trade with Japan and other Pacific Rim countries. I will be addressing this theme again in the coming months.
So, Mr. Speaker, we know precisely what we are doing. We are well prepared and we are convinced that our strategy is the best way to advance our national interest. We are actively consulting with the provinces. Indeed, our response to the softwood lumber case is a prime example of federal-provincial co-operation in a trade matter.

October 9, 1986

We have the advice of a wide array of private-sector experts and as the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) has consistently said, if our negotiations do not result in a better deal for Canada, there will be no deal. However, 1 believe it is our responsibility to try. We believe that trade problems over the past few years in such sectors as lumber, fish, pork and steel prove that existing trade rules must be improved.
We cannot improve the situation by simply turning our backs and walking away. We have the choice of negotiating to advance our interests or we can run away and let others unilaterally set the rules for us. We chose to negotiate, not because it is popular, not because it is easy, but because it is in the national interest of Canada and of Canadians.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first I would like to offer my congratulations to the Minister on being appointed to her new position. It is not possible to do so in Question Period and I am pleased to do so now.
1 would, however, note that yet again the Government, through the words of the Minister, has relied on insults with respect to her critics. She has suggested that they have no answers. I suggest that she might wish to listen, as we listened to her speech today, when we speak later next week. She will hear of the course we would be following in place of the course that is now being followed.
I would also note that I saw certain inaccuracies in the speech which has just been made, particularly with respect to GATT. As someone who attended the GATT meetings, I would have to say that there was a great deal of uneasiness and opposition expressed by European and Japanese delegates and GATT officials to the bilateral course which we were taking up with the United States. If the Minister is not aware of that, she should talk with the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) who led the delegation, or with the Minister of State for Finance (Mr. Hockin) who was there as well and could, I assume, report the same thing.
I have some questions which I would like to put very briefly, recognizing that it is not possible to have a full-scale debate at this stage. I might say that I look forward to the full-scale debate which was promised by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) when he first announced the initiative that is being taken toward the United States. This is a full-scale debate which has yet to be put before the House.
I have three questions. First, if we are concerned with such things as access to the United States, "Buy American" and a whole host of questions of restrictive protectionism within the United States, why do we not follow the route of GATT now that the GATT talks are under way after Punta del Este and carry these discussions with the United States forward with the strong support of allies who are equally concerned with each of these points which the Minister has considered in her speech? The Japanese, for instance, would be such strong allies.
The Address-Miss Carney
Second, will we finally have the mandate of Mr. Reisman made public to the House now that he has finished his first round of discussions and the Premiers have been filled in?
Third, if I may, could I please plead with the Minister to make a change in her approach and the approach of her predecessor and to take the Canadian people into the confidence of the Government in respect of precisely what is the mandate of Mr. Reisman in these talks, instead of carrying forward this cloak and dagger diplomacy which is out of place between two modern democracies?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, to address the concerns expressed by the Hon. Member, I looked again at my speaking notes. I cannot see any reference to these insults which the Hon. Member identified. I believe the only comment I made about the critics was to say that they have the responsibility to address these same realities and to tell Canadians how their policies will meet the needs of Canadians today. If asking the opposition Parties, and particularly the NDP, to put forward their policies is an insult, it speaks to the nature of the policies, not to the opportunity provided by the Government to produce them.
In answer to the specific questions raised by the Hon. Member, when he talks about the need to take allies into our discussions with the U.S., he does not seem to understand that we have a unique relationship with the U.S. It takes 78 per cent of our exports and, in turn, we are the United States, biggest customer. One province alone, Ontario, sells as much to the U.S. as does Japan. There is little to be gained by taking outside of GATT some sort of regional bloc, which he seems to be suggesting, composed of Europe, Japan, and the U.S. We are talking about GATT and we are talking about a bilateral arrangement. I also want to assure him that I thought he might have understood, or maybe he would have learned at Punta del Este that under Section 24 of the GATT these bilateral arrangements are allowed. That is why there is a European Community. That is why there is a European Free Trade Association.
I do not understand how he could indicate that Europeans were concerned about a bilateral arrangement between Canada and the U.S. when they are members of the very same kind of regional trading arrangement that allows them access to 265 million people. We, with our 26 million people, are the only industrialized country in the world that does not have secure access to a market of at least 100 million people. I think they were concerned about protectionism at the GATT; everyone is concerned about the rising tide of protectionism. However, I would suggest that the support Canada gave other countries in their objectives in the GATT will alleviate their fears.
Also, the Hon. Member asked about Simon Reisman's mandate and about taking Canadians into confidence in the negotiations. I have certainly tried to be as open as I can about the negotiations. However, I do not understand how one can

October 9, 1986

negotiate a treaty at a table in full public view. 1 do not know whether he is suggesting bringing in the television cameras or putting them on a stage to negotiate. Mr. Speaker, I should like to thank the Hon. Member for York East (Mr. Redway) for his question. First let me reassure him that the history of the reductions in tariff barriers, for instance, that has occurred in the 50 years since the great depression certainly has shown that there are more winners than losers in trade liberalization. We are infinitely better off in 1986 than we were when the process started. I think I can reassure him generally on that point.
On his specific point about whether the Government is addressing this, yes, both countries in the trade negotiations are addressing the need to have a long-term agreement-and we are talking about from now into the next century-to phase in any changes, to have the relevant adjustment programs for those who are affected, and to have training programs for those who are affected to take advantage of the jobs that will be created. Those points are being addressed in the negotiations.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will resist the temptation to try to respond to the comments of the Hon. Minister for International Trade (Miss Carney) because there are several other things I had the intention of addressing today. Debate about a major initiative of the Government is very useful, and I hope there will be more
opportunities for it to happen. My intention today is to speak, first, as the spokesperson of my Party for the environment and, second, as a western Canadian who is concerned about the problems affecting that region of Canada.
In respect of the Speech from the Throne, when it comes to environmental issues, the Throne Speech is significant for what is not in it rather than for what is in it. In the Throne Speech we have the promise of a new Environmental Protection Act. That is to be welcomed. We hope that we will soon see that legislation. Presuming that it is quality legislation-and I know that a great deal of consultation has gone into it already-we will certainly be prepared to be as co-operative as we can when the legislation comes forward, of course always depending upon the fact that there are no surprises in it of which we are not aware at this time. We will be looking forward to playing a constructively critical role in that respect.
There was also acceptable rhetoric about water quality in the Throne Speech. However, I was disappointed that very shortly after the presentation of the Throne Speech, at a meeting of Ministers of the Environment, the federal Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan) was not able to make new commitments to federal involvement in the much needed upgrading of our sewage treatment facilities across the country. I am told that some 53 per cent of sewage still goes into the environment completely untreated. That should be regarded as a national disgrace and should not be something which is subject to the usual kind of bureaucratic tinkering, as to whether we will have a few more dollars here or a few more dollars there. It is one of the least complicated environmental problems we face. It is less complicated than knowing what to do about invisible toxins in the Niagara River, for instance. It is something we know what to do about and something we could be doing. I fail to understand why the Government could not make a major announcement in that area. It would have been particularly helpful in areas suffering from high unemployment such as Quebec and Atlantic Canada where this kind of upgrading is most needed.
I said that the Throne Speech in respect of the environment was significant in what was left out. What was left out was a commitment to live up to the Progressive Conservative Party's campaign promise for a full inquiry into the nuclear industry. This is a promise of the Conservative Party which goes back to 1979. It is a promise that looked like it was going to be acted upon by the Conservative Government in 1979, but we all know that that Government did not have a chance to act on it. But the Conservatives have now been in office for two years. I have been after them to live up to the promise, a promise repeated in the election of 1984. Even after Chernobyl and the international meetings in Vienna, which the former Minister of Energy said would have to transpire before the Government would make its decision about an inquiry, we see no commitment to such an inquiry in the Throne Speech.
October 9, 1986

Unfortunately we do have a statement from the new Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Masse), not a statement made in this House, not a statement made in the Throne Speech, not a statement made to the Canadian people, not a statement even made in Canada, but a statement made by the Minister of Energy to the international meeting in Vienna. His official news release says "The Minister reaffirmed Canada's commitment to nuclear energy. Let Canada's position be clear. We are determined to use nuclear energy". That is the position taken by the new Minister of Energy in Vienna. If that is the position of the Government, why not make it absolutely clear here at home in the House of Commons to the Canadian people that that promise of the Progressive Conservative Party to initiate a full scale inquiry into the nuclear industry in Canada has been abandoned.
Other things which the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources said at that conference which I find interesting concerned food irradiation which, as we know, is at least a matter of some controversy, but not in the mind of the Minister of Energy. He said "food irradiation, for example, has become indispensable to human progress". Indispensable to human progress, Mr. Speaker. I cannot accuse the new Minister of Energy of being ambiguous about his views on nuclear energy.
I ask the Government to be more forthcoming about what official government positions are with respect to questions like food irradiation, though we had a pretty clear indication of what the Government policy will be today from the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) when he answered a question from the Hon. Member for Leeds-Grenville (Mrs. Cossitt). As far as he was concerned he was willing to accept the verdict that food irradiation was completely safe.
The view of the Government in this respect is what I call completely technocratic. It is willing to accept uncritically the prevailing confidence in that kind of technological expertise. The Tories' former ability to think critically about these kinds of technologies, displayed in 1979, has gone by the boards completely, either for internal reasons or, like so many governments before it, because of deference to the expertise in various departments. Whatever the case may be, Mr. Speaker, we have a position where that promise has been abandoned.
The Minister of Energy also said in Vienna when he was speaking about public concern and the need to alleviate public concern about the nuclear industry, "Acceptance must be based on understanding and not on propaganda." That is a good statement, but I say to the Minister of Energy, if he is interested in understanding; that if Canadian nuclear policy cannot be based on propaganda, it cannot be based on secrecy either. It cannot be based on a refusal to make major announcements and major statements of policy about the nuclear industry in the House of Commons. Understanding cannot be created when Ministers of Energy responsible for that industry refuse to create opportunities for meaningful debate, and everything happens behind closed doors.
The Address-Mr. Blaikie
As many of you will know, our response to this continuing unwillingness of the Conservative Party to live up to its promises has been to do what we can to give Canadians an opportunity to say what they think about Canada's involvement in the nuclear option. That is why the New Democratic Party announced in July that we New Democrats will be having our own inquiry and that we will be going across the country talking to people about what they think about Canada's involvement in the nuclear option.
There was mention of acid rain in the Throne Speech and Canada's continuing-I forget the exact rhetoric-determination to do something about acid rain or something like that. I am glad to see it at least got a mention, but I continue to hold my view that the position of Canada with respect to acid rain, at least in its international sense, in its trans-boundary sense with the United States, continues to be one of shameful acquiescence to the agenda of the Reagan administration. In fact, the Reagan administration has succeeded beyond its wildest dreams because it has now set the acid rain agenda for the next five years, which reaches beyond the presidency of Ronald Reagan. For the next five years all that we can hope to see with respect to progress, at least initiated by the administration, unless Congress is able to do something, is spending on research into clean coal technologies, and we have no guarantee that that will happen in any significant way, and even if it does happen that it will lead to an actual reduction in emissions.
I see that the Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan) is here. Perhaps he will have an opportunity later to tell us why-I think this might have been a mistake-the question of another trans-boundary question, that of the Niagara River pollution, was left out of the Throne Speech. That may have sent the wrong kind of signal to our American friends; not being right up there alongside acid rain as a major environmental issue with respect to Canada-U.S. relations. I find it very regrettable that that was not there alongside acid rain. I hope the Minister will take the first opportunity to indicate that that oversight should not be misinterpreted by the United States to mean any diminishing of Canada's intention to get a meaningful settlement with respect to that issue.
I want to speak now as a western Canadian about what I think is a very significant political transition happening, particularly on the prairies. It has to do with what I think to be a series of broken promises made to western Canadians over the years by the Progressive Conservative Party, promises which were believed by a majority of western Canadians and promises which led western Canadians to vote for many Conservative Members of Parliament into office over the years, and particularly during the last election. I think that the Progressive Conservative Party has seriously let down western Canada. I want to give a few examples, important examples of why that is the case.
The first one that springs to my mind, perhaps because I come from a rail town like Transcona, is the question of VIA Rail. This has been raised a number of times in the House

October 9, 1986
The Address-Mr. Blaikie
since we have returned after the summer. Still, after two years of this Government in office we do not have the new transcontinental equipment ordered. How long does it take to get up the resolve and the competency to order the equipment that everyone and his dog knows is needed if there is to be a serious possibility of a revitalized passenger rail system in this country?
I do not think anyone could argue the fact that the Government has seriously botched the future of Via Rail. This spring we saw the disgrace of legislation brought forward to put cost recovery targets on the transcontinental routes of Via Rail. The legislation would require Via Rail to meet those targets in two years. The Government knew full well that with the new equipment not even ordered it was absolutely impossible for Via Rail to meet those cost recovery targets. The only way it could meet them is with new equipment and there is no possibility of having that new equipment by the time the deadlines in the legislation come into effect. I hope we will see some change in those deadlines when the legislation comes before the House. However, the facts remains that we still have not ordered that equipment. I hope that very soon the new Minister of Transport (Mr. Crosbie) will be able to announce the real purchasing of that equipment, not just announce its intention one more time. When the Minister said half-jokingly the other day that he hoped he would get to announce that new equipment just as so many of his predecessors had, I said under my breath that I hoped he would be the last Minister to make that announcement, because I hope the next time the announcement is made it means some action will be forthcoming.
The other day we heard of the desire on the part of CN and CP to abandon literally tens of thousands of miles of rail lines. The Minister of Transport got up and said, rest assured, CN and CP would have to work within the law. What law? The law this Government intends to change? The law this Government intends to change in order to give CN and CP more freedom to do whatever they want? The Minister referred to the Canadian Transport Commission. We have every reason to believe that after the new National Transportation Act is passed there will not be anything like the CTC we have known up until this day. CN and CP, partly as a result of that new legislation and deregulation, will be able to do anything they want as long as they can show it is necessary to their being what they call competitive.
I say to all western Canadians who may have sincerely thought over the years that they had real, genuine allies over there, that they do not. They cannot have real allies in a Party which has committed itself first of all, not to western Canada but to the ideology of the market-place. In the final analysis, if the market-place dictates the extinction of western Canada, or the extinction of the family farm, or the extinction of whatever the market-place dictates is next up for obsolescence, you cannot really have allies among people whose first commitment is to that kind of ideology.
Let me speak for a minute about the family farm. The one thing that should shake up a lot of people in this country, particularly people of a small "c" conservative bent, if you will-people who think that the family farm represents an enduring kind of institution, a cultural value structure which is to be regarded as one of the high points of Canadian life-it is that if the family farm is vulnerable, if it can be dispensed with, if it can be sacrificed on the altar of the international market-place and of so-called competition, then everything else is vulnerable. No one is safe.
What kind of response to that have we from this Government? We have a transition program to help farmers off the land. Why? Because farming is no longer regarded as a vocation by governments, it is regarded strictly as a business. No more talk about relationships with the land. The land is just something to be pumped and milked with fertilizers and pesticides and everything else you can get your hands on to get the highest possible yield to make the biggest possible buck. The problem, of course, is that even doing that, under the current international economic system the farmers cannot make enough money to survive.
Instead of coming down hard on the international system and on the banks and others who are doing this to our farmers, we see a look of regret on the face of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) and others that this has happened. They say they are going to do what they can within the existing fiscal framework, but they are not going to take on the forces which are destroying the family farm in western Canada. The family farm is not just being destroyed, the very ecological basis on which our agricultural sector is based is being destroyed. I refer to the report by the Senate on soil erosion and other evidence which has been piling up over the years, that the way we have allowed our agricultural sector to develop is a recipe for disaster. The chickens are starting to come home to roost on that particular way of farming and the farmers, in my view, should be the last to be victimized by the consequences, instead of the first, which is the case right now.

My government recognizes fully the essential relationship between a healthy environment and the quality of Canadian life. October 9, 1986

Member not agree that, while obviously pollution in the Niagara River is terribly important and must be dealt with, pollution in the St. Clair River must also be dealt with, as must pollution in the St. Lawrence River? I would also like to thank the constituents of Stormont-Dundas. I have enjoyed representing them in this House during the last two years and I look forward to continuing to be their representative here in the future. It is a great honour and one which I appreciate very much. All of you in Stormont-Dundas have my utmost respect. Stormont- Dundas is a riding in eastern Ontario less than an hour's drive from Cornwall and Montreal. Tourism is one of our most important industries and we have several very attractive features in our area. I want to briefly mention a number of them.
The St. Lawrence Seaway goes through my riding with a lock at Iroquois in the western part, in Dundas County. Close by in Iroquois is Carmen House, one of the oldest dwellings in the area, built around 1825. Also close by in Dundas is Dundela, the home of the McIntosh apple which has become world renowned. East of Morrisburg is auto Wonderland, and Prehistoric World on Upper Canada Road. There is also Upper Canada Village, a reconstructed pioneer village that
many of us have visited several times. Further east toward Ingleside is a wildlife sanctuary which at this time of year has thousands of Canada geese and is truly an outstanding place to visit for any photographer or family.
In Cornwall, there is Rossi Glass, United Counties Museum, the R. H. Sanders generating station, Inverarden Regency Cottage Museum, a building that was built in 1816. There is the Charlottenburgh waterfowl sanctuary toward the eastern part of my riding near Lancaster, the Nor'westers Loyalist Museum in Williamstown, and the St. Raphael's church ruins in the heart of a Scottish community which is celebrating its bicentennial this year.
We are also quite fortunate in having several agricultural fairs around the riding. In June there is the Maxville Fair, in July there is the Avonmore Fair and in August there is Williamstown, South Mountain, Chesterville, while in September there is Newington. As well as these outstanding agricultural fairs there is the world famous Glengarry Highland Games on the first Saturday of August each year.
There are approximately 1,900 farms in my community, 43 per cent of which are dairy operations, 26 per cent beef cattle, and 12 per cent which cultivate small grains. When our nation's shoppers spend over $500 million per week in purchasing Canadian food products, we know the importance of our agricultural sector, not only for Stormont-Dundas but for all of Canada.
The Government's Speech from the Throne emphasizes Canada's commitment to agriculture and the role it plays in our national economy. As our Minister has recently outlined, we are aware of the present difficulties and we are definitely committed to work toward solving many of these problems, with the assistance and co-operation of provincial Governments and farm organizations, to help alleviate the hardship that many of our farm communties have been experiencing. The Throne Speech makes it clear, in making its commitment to Canadian agriculture, that the Government will spare no effort in seeking to protect the interests of Canada's farming community in the face of unfair competiton outside the country.
In co-operation with the provinces, we have recently committed $1 billion of assistance to our grain farmers in Canada. As the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) stated a few minutes ago, since coming to office the Government has brought forward over 300 separate initiatives totalling more than $5 billion which will benefit Canadian agriculture. The Government has effectively removed all sales tax and excise tax from all diesel and gasoline farm fuels, through a system of rebates. To date, some $100 million in low-interest loans has been approved under the new Commodity Based Loan Program. The Government has worked for lower interest rates, saving farmers millions of dollars in interest. We now have farm credit loans with the lowest rates since 1979.
Canada now has a national Red Meat Stabilization Program. The federal Government's commitment of $1.5
October 9, 1986

billion over a five-year period to its new dairy policy will provide the dairy industry with a stability it has not enjoyed since 1980. The 1985 Budget provided farmers with an immediate $500,000 capital gains exemption, effectively eliminating capital gains on the sale of most farms.
An essential part of our economic renewal program is tax reform. The capital gains initiative was one of the beginning steps of this tax reform. Federal tax reform is a top economic and social priority of the Progressive Conservative Government. A principal objective of the changes made so far has been to broaden the tax base and lower tax rates. We must restore a healthier balance among the personal, corporate and sales taxes, and specifically reverse the trend which has resulted in a greater reliance on personal income tax. The Government's further consideration of tax reform will have fairness as one of its guiding principles.
The Government is determined to move forward in a careful and co-ordinated way to ensure that the tax system is made less complex wherever possible. In developing our options for reform, we must also ensure that our tax system provides a strong and positive framework for economic growth and the expansion of job opportunities for all Canadians.
The Government has been examining broader options for the more complex reform of the federal tax system, including a business transfer tax which would possibly replace the federal sales tax. At the present time, there are several inequities in the federal sales tax and this area needs our immediate attention.
Since the Budget in February, the pace of comprehensive tax reform in the United States has escalated and they will soon be bringing in new tax measures which will have to spur us on in our tax reform program. Canadians must remain competitive with our American counterparts.
The Speech from the Throne noted the Government's concern about increasing concentration of corporate ownership, particularly where take-overs serve to increase corporate size without creating new jobs or stimulating economic growth in Canada. Tax reform will most likely deal with this concern.

Since we came to power, we have introduced important measures aimed at regenerating the Canadian economy. These measures have helped to restore confidence, create jobs, bring down interest rates and reduce the deficit. In September 1984, 11.7 per cent of the labour force was out of work. Today, the unemployment rate is down to 9.7 per cent.

Economic renewal has not been even across Canada. Certain parts of Ontario have experienced a tremendous boom, especially in the Toronto area where the housing boom has been quite astounding. Our programs will have to consider those other parts of our country that have been less fortunate.
Presenting statistics on unemployment has caused problems and, at times, controversy. The official unemployment rate in
Address-Mr. Warner
certain areas does not reflect the jobless rate. I represent one of those areas. The official rate of unemployment in Stormont-Dundas is approximately 8 per cent or 9 per cent, but no one in my area takes this figure very seriously because they know that it reflects the unemployment figures for all of eastern Ontario, including Ottawa. It also, does not take into consideration such factors as participation rate or those who are on welfare and available for work.
Yesterday in the House there was some controversy about the jobless rate in Manicouagan. I am sure that when the people in Manicouagan speak of a jobless rate, they understand it is closer to 37 per cent than it is to the official 15.8 per cent. They are living there. They know they do not have jobs. It is not 15.8 per cent because that does not consider the participation rate, the people who are employable and on welfare-

In the Cornwall area, we have been quite successsful in creating jobs for many of the unemployed people. Address-Mr. Warner
The Government is resolved to defend and strengthen the Canadian family which is the foundation of Canadian society. In many families in Stormont-Dundas, as in the rest of the country, both parents are now working. Adequate quality child care must be available. We look forward to receiving the Martin Committee Report on Child Care which will most likely be followed by discussions with the provinces, business and labour. I look forward to a co-operative approach from all the Parties in solving this difficult problem.
The Government is determined to take effective action against child sexual abuse, violent forms of pornography involving women and children, child prostitution and the serious and growing threat posed by the traffic in illegal drugs. Current indications are that Canadians now have a $10 billion a year drug problem. That is equivalent to $400 for every man, woman and child in Canada. This situation is intolerable and poses a serious threat to our society. All levels of Government and all Canadians must be concerned with this problem.
I would like to congratulate the law enforcement officers operating in Stormont-Dundas and Glengarry for their efforts in thwarting drug trafficking. Special congratulations go to the City of Cornwall police and their Chief, Claude Shaver, and Deputy Police Chief, Denis O'Neill, for their recent efforts.
The Government recognizes the essential relationship between a healthy environment and the quality of life. An industry-labour-Government task force will be preparing recommendations concerning the workplace environment. Following its recommendations, the Government will propose legislation to establish a workplace hazardous materials information system. Our environment is fragile and its protection requires the assistance of all Canadians.

The Government wants to adapt social measures to the real needs of the people. Canada's future is its young people, and the Speech from the Throne is emphatic about increasing opportunities for this important group in our population.
The Government is happy about the drop in youth unemployment, from 18.4 per cent on election day to 15 per cent today. However, much remains to be done.

The Government will be seeking the co-operation of the provinces and the private sector to enhance job opportunities and to encourage the participation and involvement of young Canadians in productive and challenging initiatives. The Government will be working with the provinces, the private sector and voluntary organizations to develop measures to ensure that all Canadians have access to the literacy skills which are the prerequisites for participation in a developed economy. Our local problem with illiteracy was recently brought to my attention by journalist Huguette Burroughs, whose concern I sincerely appreciate.
Today Canadian youth have benefited from numerous Government initiatives including the Canadian Jobs Strategy
and Challenge '86. In 1985 the Student Employment Centre in Stormont-Dundas placed 1,200 student. That was a new record for student placement in our riding. In 1986 the Student Employment Centre placed 1,400 students. Other jobs were created throughout our riding at a most successful rate.
The Government Speech from the Throne recognizes the importance of Canada's multicultural and multiracial communities. The reality of Canada today calls for all facets of our national life to reflect the vital and distinctive nature of Canadian society. Increased immigration levels, particularly among business immigrants, will have a positive effect on Canada's well being. These people will not only help to create jobs for themselves but for other unemployed Canadians as well. Although many of our ethnic communities are relatively small, their contribution to our society is very substantial.
I am very proud to have been involved in the formation of our annual Multicultural Festival. Sultan Jessa, a former citizen of the year in Cornwall, will be chairing the fifth annual festival to be held in Cornwall on June 28, 1987. At least 12 ethnic communities will be represented by performances, displays, food and beverages. The festival provided the foundation for Worldfest/Festimonde. In its third edition next year, Chairman Denis Carr expects several outstanding performing groups from around the world. They will be in Cornwall from June 26 to Canada Day, July 1. Worldfest/Festimonde is destined to be one of Canada's outstanding multicultural events and it certainly will have the encouragement of our Government.
The Speech from the Throne acknowledged the tens of thousands of Canadians who serve their communities and their country as volunteers. Further support was pledged to encourage the growth of volunteerism in our society. Our Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) recently announced his approval of grants totalling $3.3 million for several national voluntary organizations to assist them in the cost of operating their national offices and carrying out national activities during the upcoming year. These organizations include Big Brothers of Canada, Boys and Girls Clubs of Canada, CNIB, Family Service Canada, YMCA. YWCA and many others. A 1983 study estimated that the value of volunteer time in Canada was worth $2 billion. Altogether, charitable contributions and volunteer time would be worth in excess of $5 billion today. The volunteers in our community are very valuable and will continue to have our support. I continue to ask all the people in my area to help me with my work: municipal politicians, provincial politicians and our successful contingent.
The Speech from the Throne is just a bench-mark in our progress. We look forward to a much better community in the time to come.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened with interest to the Eton. Member's speech on the Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne. I would like to ask him two questions.
In his speech he took time to mention the multicultural and immigrant community in his riding. He mentioned the attributes that these people give to life in his community and, in fact, what they have brought to the country. I would first like to ask the Hon. Member what his thoughts are with respect to the infamous report written by some of his colleagues in Toronto with respect to using-and I use that word deliberately and in the negative sense-those very immigrant communities and ethnocultural organizations to the political benefit of the Conservative Party of Canada. How does that fit into the statements he has just made?
With respect to entrepreneurial immigrants, I would like to know what his thoughts are with respect to the following. The Conservative Party has doubled the quota for business immigrants. That is something which is key and integral to the immigration program. It is something which my Party supports. However, we support it only if it forms one part of the over-all immigration program. What is happening in posts around the world is that because of the doubling of the immigration quota for business applicants, resources and personnel are being shifted away from other operations of the immigration program to satisfy these quotas which have been targetted by the Government. Hong Kong produces one-half of the total number of business immigrants who come into Canada. Because there are not additional resources in place to handle these numbers, individuals are being removed from the family class and family assistance class in order to satisfy the business class quotas. Is the Hon. Member in favour of this practice? Would he like to see a cost recovery program put in place in terms of business immigrants who are willing and able to pay an additional $125 visa charge for services rendered? I ask this with the proviso that it does not negatively affect the chances of a family wishing to immigrate, since personnel are being shifted in order to meet the immigration quotas for business applicants.
I am interested to hear what the Hon. Member has to say with respect to the Toronto report. I would also like to hear what he has to say with respect to the whole philosophy of business applicants and how that situation negatively affects the delays in terms of family class immigrants, something on which the Standing Committee on Labour, Employment and Immigration took great pains to submit a report to the Minister in June.

Mr. Speaker, with respect to the Hon. Member's first question, I am not familiar with the report to which he refers. In my riding I do not actively participate in any sort of scheme of the type mentioned by the Hon. Member. As I mentioned in my speech, the ethnic community in my riding is fairly small and formed of outstanding citizens. Many of them are professionals, and most of them are quite active in volunteer efforts. They are very prominent in many ways outside their own professions and businesses.
Address-Mr. Warner
With respect to the Hon. Member's other remark, I support the entrepreneur class immigrant. This encourages foreign investors to come into the country. The Hon. Member mentioned a doubling of the figure from 2,000 to 4,000. I believe we could consider an even higher target. The Hon. Member also mentioned the complications with respect to Hong Kong. Hong Kong has the potential to supply several times the maximum number of entrepreneurs, and there will probably be considerable pressure placed on the rest of the world in the next two or three years to try to absorb some of these immigrants.
A cost recovery program is something which I think can be considered. At the moment I really do not know what the Minister or his Department is considering. However, this type of immigrant has the financial ability to pay for any costs incurred. Most likely they would be quite willing to pay those costs.
At the present time there are some unscrupulous operators of various kinds, such as business consultants or travel agents, who charge a fee to assist a person coming into Canada. These people being assisted are paying fees, some as high as $12,000, for a service which is of absolutely no use. At the present time the service is provided free by the Government.
I think the Hon. Member's suggestion should be relayed to the Minister and his Department for further consideration. It merits further consideration.

October 9, 1986

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Speech from the Throne generally provides the Government with an occasion to take stock, to report on the progress of the past and to set the course for the future. Of course, a Speech from the Throne is not expected to give minute details or even a budget. However, it does afford the Government an opportunity to set forth its vision and course for future direction.
The Prime Minister's assessment of what his Government has achieved does not seem to find support in fact. Except for some of the major urban areas of the Golden Horseshoe, and possibly Ottawa and Montreal as well, the rest of the country is hardly thriving the way it should in a period of what might be called recovery, world-wide recovery after a devastating world-wide recession. If we analyse area by area the record of Tory promises and Tory fulfilments, I suggest we are even less impressed.
As a Liberal Member of Parliament my job has been to monitor the responsibilities and acitivities of the Secretary of State of Canada (Mr. Crombie), and I do this for the Official Opposition. The confusion and failure of the Tory Government, its incompetence and lack of concern for this vast area, is shown by the fact that in two years I have seen two Secretaries of State come and go, and a third one has been served up for inevitable embarrassment and humiliation because his Government fails to put its money where its mouth has been. The Cabinet of which he is a part has financially savaged the areas under the Secretary of State and betrayed its promises. Not only have we seen two Secretaries of State go by in two years, but Deputy Ministers of the Department of the Secretary of State have also passed through the revolving door. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) has served up a third Deputy Minister as well.
All those involved in the areas for which the Secretary of State is responsible cannot help but suffer from the fact that we are now on our third Minister and our third Deputy Minister in two years. This is a federal Government portfolio that relates to some very heavy responsibilities. To name just a few, it relates to the 52,000 charitable organizations in the voluntary sector, to the Department of Citizenship, to the one in every eight Canadians who is disabled or handicapped, to the realms of human rights and official languages and to the more than one million students, professors and administrators in our universities and colleges. I have named only a few of the
areas for which the Secretary of State is responsible, the portfolio in which there has been a revolving door. Today I want to focus on just one of those areas, that of post-secondary education.

It is now two years since the Conservative Government came to power. If we look at what the Government has done, we see that post-secondary education in Canada is going through a serious crisis. The measures taken by the Government in the education sector are alarming, to say the least. However, the worst part is that these measures give the impression that this Government has no intention of acting on its responsibilities to young Canadians.

On the one hand, the Government acknowledges that we must do all we can to enable Canada to become more competitive and productive in order to survive economically and culturally. It even takes steps through so-called free trade negotiations to propel us at great speed into that very competition. Then on the other hand, at the very same time as it is thrusting us so rapidly into world competition, the Government is disarming our country for such a battle for national survival by allowing our educational system to drift into a state of demoralization, decay and despair, and is speeding up that process by deliberately setting priorities which retard research and the quest for excellence. It is as simple as that.
This is not a wilful act on the part of the Government to sell out Canada so that we end up as servants of foreign economic masters by cutting back on research and education, any more than in the name of economy and fiscal restraint during the Great Depression, Britain's Neville Chamberlain wilfully intended to sell out Britain to her enemies by cutting back on her military growth. Of course he did not do it intentionally. He was just looking after the deficit. However, just as the Battle of Britain was nearly lost, we shall lose the battle for Canadian economic and cultural survival unless this process and our priorities are fully reversed and unless the present laissez-faire approach is replaced by real leadership.

This overview of the measures taken by the Progressive Conservative Government may seem excessively negative and partisan. However, if we remember the promises this Government made and the measures it took subsequently, it is obvious that it has deliberately abandoned post-secondary education. If anyone remembers the promises made by the Progressive Conservatives during the 1984 election campaign, it must be the leaders of the Canadian Association of University Teachers. Responding to questions by CAUT, the Progressive Conservative Party made a commitment to maintain the formula set down in the 1977 accord for calculating transfer payments to the provinces for post-secondary education.
Furthermore, CAUT leaders remember clearly that the Progressive Conservatives made a solemn promise to double the federal Government's assistance for research.
October 9, 1986



No one could therefore be more disappointed and dismayed than the members of the Canadian Association of University Teachers to witness the course of events of the last two years.
The passage of Bill C-96 capping growth of Established Programs Financing transfer payments to the provinces at a level of 5 per cent, barely inflation, and bringing this into effect for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1987, not only broke the election promises made by Conservative Members to maintain the funding formula but broke the existing pending federal-provincial agreement before the funding formula expired. It was not only a breach of promise, it was even a breach of contract.
The planning of post-secondary education must, by nature, be long term, and anyone who is familiar with the administration of a university or a college knows that long-term planning must be used. The embarrassments caused by such a breach of promise both to the provinces and to the educational institutions are understandably acute. The assault on Canadian postsecondary education was further exacerbated by federal decisions in other vital areas.
Spokesmen on behalf of the Canadian Association of University Teachers, such as Dr. Arnold Naimark, have pointed out that the latest financing decisions made by the present Government condemn research granting councils to ending up with less money in real terms in the future than at the present. Planning ahead will be less predictable as uncertainty is introduced by matching grant formulae. Instead of the percentage of the GNP for research growing to 2.5 per cent, all evidence points to a freeze at 1.3 per cent. Again, those are more broken promises.
Other reinforcing evidence proving that this constitutes the real policy of the Government is seen in its decisions to freeze the level of the student loans, to cut back on training seats in community colleges by 40 per cent, to close many campus employment offices and to cut the budget of the Minister of State for Youth (Mr. Charest) to purely ceremonial levels. It is small wonder that this has caused a cry of alarm.

The Government doesn't know where it's going with its policies. It is not as though the recession were a perfect mystery. Alarm bells were sounded in report after report. The Johnson Report, the Macdonald Commission and reports from many of the provinces confirmed the seriousness of the problem.
Attention has been called to the diminishing level of funds spent per student, the deterioration of physical plants to serve them, the retardation of research, and the declining morale of faculty, administrators, and students alike. Representatives of all these groups have repeatedly witnessed these facts in speeches, in articles, and in testimony before committees of the
The Address-Mr. de Corneille
House and of the Senate. The Canadian Association of University Teachers has been at the forefront of such representations.
One of the most dramatic efforts to arouse public concern was courageously voiced by the Chief Justice of Canada, the Right Hon. Brian Dickson, on May 30, 1986. Quotations from his speech are a succinct summary and eloquently articulate the matter. The Chief Justice quoted remarks made by Dr. Andrew MacKay, President of Dalhousie University, someone who we would all concede has some knowledge of the problems facing universities in the land. I should like to quote from Dr. MacKay who in turn was quoted by the Chief Justice:
Fiscal restraints have brought student-faculty ratios perilously high at many of our institutions. They have made it nearly impossible for. us to bring in bright new minds to teach our students and undertake research. Our libraries are suffering for want of appropriate acquisitions. Most of our scientific, technical and computing equipment for teaching is obsolete.
Our physical plant is generally in desperate need of repair. And many of us have found it necessary to turn away students we would previously have admitted to our core programs in the arts and sciences because we can no longer do work of satisfactory quality except by limiting numbers.
Then, expressing his own views, Chief Justice Brian Dickson continued:
Let me speak first to governments, provincial and federal. Please do not choke off the funding of universities. Canada must have good universities with outstanding teachers and world-class research facilities. Second-class funding of universities will inevitably lead to second-class teachers, second-class students and, ultimately, a second-class nation.
It has been said by many people that education is too important to be left to educators. That may be true. But it is also true that education is too important to be left to Ministers of Finance. Universities desperately require funds to perform their great mission in democratic societies. Governments spend billions of dollars every year on all manner of projects, many worth while, others not so worth while. In my opinion, money spent on minds will never be money misspent.
As the Liberal critic of the Secretary of State, I have repeatedly brought such representations to the floor of the House of Commons during Question Period. I have also spoken on them at length in speeches I made on May 5, May 6, May 8, June 10, and June 16. My colleagues have also spoken vigorously, so there cannot be doubt in anyone's mind about the Government's awareness of the problems associated with Bill C-96. However, the Conservative administration was determined to pass the Bill without modification. We see that by its repeated use of closure; that demonstrates it only too clearly.

The Government has only two arguments to explain why it failed to fulfil its promises and to justify its criminal negligence vis-a-vis the future of education in Canada. It can recall the need for bringing down the deficit, and it can also maintain that in any case, funds transferred to the provinces never reach the rightful recipient-in this case, educational institutions.

In the case of the former argument, the Conservatives cannot claim that when they made their promises and commitments to the electorate they did not know about the annual

October 9, 1986
The Address-Mr. de Corneille
national deficit and the national debt. In the course of the election campaign they repeatedly cited these statistics to condemn what they called Liberal mismanagement of national spending. At the same time they promised better things for both educational EPF transfers and research. Furthermore, the issue is surely one of priorities.
Through their spokesmen the provinces have expressed dismay. Many feel that the unilateral federal action taken in Bill C-96 transfers the deficit from the federal Government to the provinces and, in the case of poorer provinces, to the poor who will inevitably suffer. It also reinforces the thesis that the Government places a low priority on post-secondary education and research. However, if the future of Canada's economy and culture is linked to education and research, infrastructure, and standards which are now deteriorating-and I believe it is and every thinking person knows it is-then federal government policy in this area is surely subject to question if not downright condemnation.
The second excuse, which the Government could put forward for its low priority on education and research, but is afraid to mention except in whispers, is that federal funds do not always reach their intended destinations, namely, education, because the provinces do not always pass them on. That argument, however, would only affect federal government policy on EPF transfers and does not explain the Government's failure to provide moneys for research, student loans, et cetera. Morever, in the case of EPF tranfers, the Conservative Government has simply abdicated any kind of creative approach to dealing with the question. It has walked away from suggestions from the royal commission, from the proposals of the Johnson report, and from those submitted earlier by CAUT. It has done nothing to deal with what is clearly a growing national crisis that threatens not only the future of countless individuals but our potential and capacity to survive as a viable nation.

Criticism comes easily, but action is what really counts. This is why the Leader of the Opposition has set up a national task force on post-secondary education, of which I am chairman. The task force has begun its work and will report its findings to the Leader of the Opposition, to the caucus, and to the Party before the Liberal Party national convention scheduled for late November this year. On the basis of briefs submitted from every region of the country I will be in a position to recommend options taking into consideration the crisis to be resolved, and other options which will make it possible for Canada to begin the 21st century with all the necessary assets to survive.

Condemnation is not enough. Leadership is required. For this reason the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner) has initiated a national task force on post-secondary education. We must not lose sight of the fact that students represent the ultimate reason for which education exists. That
is why I say a laissez-faire approach will not protect the disadvantaged.
I would like to close my remarks with words spoken by the Leader of the Opposition at the Atlantic Policy Conference in June, 1986:
I am going to initiate a review of post-secondary education funding to improve standards once again in co-operation and in negotiation with the provinces to ensure that we have minimum standards right across the country in terms of mobility, accessibility, research and student aid. These are going to have to happen. It is a national problem and it needs a solution with a national perspective.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have just had a wonderful example of what happens to members of a political Party when they move from the government side to the Opposition side of this Chamber. Every year for years when the Liberals were the Government representations were made to the Government by the Association of Canadian Universities, by the Canadian Association of University Teachers, and by the provincial Governments, pointing out that when it came to one of the subjects on which the Hon. Member spent some time, scientific research and development, that if you took all the countries belonging to the OECD, and Japan, only Italy spent a smaller percentage of its gross national product on scientific research and development. Every year Members of the Opposition, both Conservative and New Democrat, joined in that criticism and appealed to the Liberal Government to do better. Nothing happened, and Canada still remains at the bottom of the totem pole.
The Member talked about support for post-secondary education. I remind the Member that it was the Liberal Government that ended the fifty-fifty cost-sharing of postsecondary education with the six and five program. It put a cap on what the federal Government would contribute. It was the federal Government which ended the fifty-fifty costsharing, fifty-fifty for the have provinces and substantially more than fifty-fifty for the have-not provinces, which brought in the Established Programs Financing Act. Members of my Party, myself included, warned the Liberal Government that, not only would this cut-back on the federal Government's contribution in theory but in fact, the provinces would no longer be required to use that money, which came in a lump sum for post-secondary education and health programs on that, but could use it to build roads if that was politically advantageous to them, and is exactly what some of the provinces did.
All these complaints and appeals were ignored by the Liberal Government. Now the Liberal Party is in opposition. Now we hear all the speeches. Now we get the quotations from the briefs presented by the scientific organizations and by the university organizations. What assurances do we, the people of Canada have-I hope it never happens if we have another Liberal Government-that it will live up to the kinds of speeches and promises which the Hon. Member has made
October 9, 1986

tonight when the Liberals did not do it in all the years they were in power before?

speechtext: First, let us take the changeover from the system of payments which was 50 per cent from the federal Government for post-secondary education matched by 50 per cent from the provinces. If he were to tell the whole story and try to understand what the federal Government was doing at that time, it was trying to respond to the province's complaints that post-secondary education was a matter, under the Constitution, within the sole jurisdiction of the provinces to administer. Second, the Government was trying to argue that by putting it on a fifty-fifty basis, the rich provinces could put up 50 cents for every 50 cents the federal Government put up. But when you have a situation where a poor province is involved, a poor province cannot put up that 50 cents per dollar. If you have a province that has a smaller budget and less industry, such as some of our provinces and I will not name specific ones, it is unable to put up much money at all for post-secondary education. Sure the federal Government could match it, but it would be a small amount. Whereas, if you have a province that is well off, like Quebec or Ontario, it would be able to put up large amounts of money which the federal Government would then match. That was what was wrong with the matching system. It was not fair to the poor provinces. It was not fair to the young people in the poor provinces. That was the reason arguments were made for changing from a system which was a 50 cent match, Fifty-fifty, to a system with a formula that was supposed to help us bring, through block payments and through transfer payments, a much fairer presentation sharing of funds to the various provinces and, therefore, to the poor people in the poor provinces. That was the nefarious reason for trying to bring about that change.
