subtopic: GOVERNMENT EXPENDITURES-PRIME MINISTER'S TRAVEL ENTOURAGE. (B) BUTLER'S DUTIES
GOVERNMENT EXPENDITURES-PRIME MINISTER'S TRAVEL ENTOURAGE. (B) BUTLER'S DUTIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, twice this week we have had a most serious controversy raised in the House. The issues involve the butler and maid of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney). However, the Prime Minister chooses not to call these people a butler and a maid. They are nobodies as far as he is concerned. As a matter of fact, he gave an interview in which Canadian Press quotes him as saying: "1 didn't take a butler, I didn't take anybody." If I was the Prime Minister's butler I would be insulted because, like at Speedy Muffler, the gentleman is a somebody, in my view. However, that is not really the point.
The point is, of course, that the Prime Minister needs the utmost in security around him. He needs people who are really qualified to make sure that the place is top-notch, security wise. So we have this James Bond butler working for the Prime Minister. He is not really a butler but a butler in disguise. We are told that he is in fact a combination stunt man, James Bond and butler all rolled into one. He should have that, because our Prime Minister deserves the best. If you do not believe me, just have a look and see what he has. Surely you will believe it then.
The Prime Minister used an L-1011 to go to Asia when a previous Prime Minister made do with a plane half that size. The Prime Minister travels on Parliament Hill with five cars. Not one car like you or I, not driving a Chevette like I do, but five cars, one of them a Cadillac. The front of the Parliament Buildings looks like a used car lot because of the attitude of the Prime Minister. Perhaps Gary Lautens said it best:
It is a well known fact, if you watch James Bond movies, that foreign agents will resort to anything to hit their target. One of their favourite weapons is Exploding Underwear.
The way it works is simple. A head of state gets up in the morning and, if he has no valet to check his personal clothing, slips right into a of pair exploding underpants without a second thought.
Pow! There go the Jockeys, et cetera, up in a puff of smoke. Especially the et ceteras.
We would not want that to happen to our Prime Minister. That is why we have such qualified people to work for him as butlers. Remember, the Prime Minister said he was not a butler, he was a nobody.
We have qualified butlers to assist the Prime Minister in his task of leading the world. Yes indeed, the Right Hon. Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) told the House of Commons that during the trip in question an agreement was reached to have Canada become part of the G-7, which had never been done before. Would you believe it? This was achieved because of the butler. Perhaps because of the maid as well, I do not want to be partisan. Far be it from me to be partisan on such an issue. The Prime Minister deserves the best and he has the best, courtesy of the Canadian people.
The issue facing the Prime Minister today is not whether or not he took a butler with him on a trip. I think it is extravagant but if he thinks it is all right, let him do it and he can justify it to the Canadian people later. What I do object to is the fact that we cannot get consistent answers out of the Government.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT EXPENDITURES-PRIME MINISTER'S TRAVEL ENTOURAGE. (B) BUTLER'S DUTIES
speechtext: You mean the truth?

subtopic: GOVERNMENT EXPENDITURES-PRIME MINISTER'S TRAVEL ENTOURAGE. (B) BUTLER'S DUTIES
speechtext: I do not know, perhaps. We hear a statement from the Prime Minister which is contradicted by his Chief of Staff, who is contradicted by the Department of External Affairs, who is further contradicted by two cabinet Ministers on the floor of this House. Contradictory statements made simultaneously about an issue can only mean one thing, that at least some of them are, shall we say, inaccurate. Perhaps Professor Jean-Luc Pepin at the University of Ottawa said it best when he said that the Prime Minister had an acute need to embellish the truth.

speakeroldname: Mr. Gordon Towers (Parliamentary Secretary to Solicitor General of Canada):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Solicitor General of Canada
subtopic: GOVERNMENT EXPENDITURES-PRIME MINISTER'S TRAVEL ENTOURAGE. (B) BUTLER'S DUTIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in answering the Hon. Member, I hope that my calibre of response will be better than his calibre of questioning. I wish to impress upon him that security protection is granted by the Canadian Government to specific categories of individuals. The RCMP has the lead role in co-ordinating this protection. Approximately 250 person years are dedicated to VIP security duty with additional members detailed as required.
The RCMP has advised successive Prime Ministers that security must extend beyond the physical security of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and his family to also include security of information and sensitive conversations, whether with close personal staff or with other officials, be they domestic or foreign. These security considerations become even more important when the Prime Minister travels abroad representing Canada.
The RCMP security office works hand-in-hand with foreign and domestic security officials as well as personnel in the
October 9, 1986

Prime Minister's office to ensure that transportation, accommodation, meeting sites, documents and communications are secured. The RCMP also stresses the importance of having close personal and domestic staff with appropriate security clearances to ensure that all of the other security measures put in place by the RCMP are not compromised. The RCMP can ensure security of personnel and information only if all persons are properly security cleared. When the Prime Minister is discussing matters of sensitivity, we do not want hotel personnel wandering in and out serving tea and cookies.
As the Solicitor General (Mr. Kelleher) stated in the House on October 6:
-what the Government does on Prime Ministerial travel is dictated in large measure by security requirements for our Prime Minister and his aides and for the people who meet with him. This is a fundamental requirement."
No reasonable person today should deny the need to provide security for heads of state and heads of government. We are constantly reminded by the RCMP, and rightly so, of the need to provide a high level of security at all times while the Prime Minister is on extended travel. This includes having trained and secure support staff who form an integral part of the overall security arrangements.
What would Members opposite say, what would Canadians think, if sensitive information concerning Canada's economic interest or national security, to give two examples, became common knowledge because we did not take the precautions advised by the RCMP protective security experts? We should all know the answer to that, Mr. Speaker. It is clear that in making arrangements for travel abroad for the Prime Minister, the Government has taken the best advice of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police and acted accordingly.

subtopic: INDIAN AFFAIRS-FUNDING OF PROGRAMS. (B) BAND FUNDING INQUIRY
INDIAN AFFAIRS-FUNDING OF PROGRAMS. (B) BAND FUNDING INQUIRY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise this evening to express my dissatisfaction with the answer given to me by the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. McKnight) yesterday in the House. Before doing so, I would like to offer my apologies to the Minister. I did say that I would get some documents to him, but I did not get them to him in adequate time for him to fully absorb the contents and import of them. I hope that over the next few days he will allow himself the time to study those documents because I am sure his eyes will be opened by them.
In his answer yesterday the Minister stated that there had not been cut-backs to funding in the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development. He also stated that to his knowledge no signed agreement or contract had been broken. I believe that the documents which I have delivered to the Minister will convince him that the contrary is so. These documents show that contribution agreements signed on behalf of the Government of Canada were indeed broken, specifically in the instance of bands in the Manitoba region which received less than the funds to which they were entitled under the contribution agreement.
Adjournment Debate
These funds were not delivered. They were not undelivered by a matter of inadvertence, they remained undelivered by a deliberate decision of officials of his Ministry. Any agreement, be it between individuals, or between Governments, or between different levels of Governments, contains clauses which allow for its revision and review. I believe that the opportunty has always existed under contribution arrangements for representatives of the Department to go back to bands and state the difficulties they are in and state the reasons why they would like to see funding not delivered or delivered in another fiscal year.
Almost as offensive as the breaking of agreements in this instance is the way in which those agreements were breached. It appears from my discussions with chiefs of Manitoba bands, and a former official of the Department in Manitoba, that there was not only no consultation with the bands which were affected and whose treasuries were substantially impaired by these withholding of funds, they were not even informed of the fact that the funds had been retained from them.
The impact of these actions holds the most serious consequences for the relationship of the Government, and the Minister, now that he is in that position, with the bands of this country. The whole basis of the relationship of Government with the indigenous people of this country is one of trust. It is even enshrined in the law of the land, that there is a trust toward the indigenous people of Canada from the Government and through the Ministry of Indian Affairs.
The result of these actions was that the trust has been very substantially eroded, perhaps beyond the point where the Government can re-establish it. The results at the band level were serious. A million dollars was clawed back in the last fiscal year from the operation and maintenance budget of the Education Department in Manitoba. A million dollars was: "Frozen to your mandatory deficit". The ultimate fate of that million dollars was to be returned to headquarters.
Even worse, there was a $4 million shortfall of which only 18 per cent has been funded in the Budget for education, operation and maintenance. Of course, that is mostly for the maintenance and repair of schools. That shortfall was because of the headquarter's doubts about the validity of the Capital Asset Inventory System valuation of the assets of the schools that were being maintained. Those doubts were subsequently resolved, but only 18 per cent of the shortfall has been granted to the region.
The Ward Mallette Report documented a misuse of the Payable at Year End procedure, which records obligations owing by the Department at the end of the fiscal year. I regret to inform the Minister that that malpractice is continuing on a scale that can only be described as high, wide and handsome.
The documents that I have submitted to the Minister show the shocking distortions of fiscal responsibility which occur when these actions are taken. They talk in such terms as early

October 9, 1986
Adjournment Debate
recapitalization of assets, which frankly means if you do not maintain something it will have to be replaced much sooner.
Finally, the Minister made a spurious comparison in the House yesterday-I am sure unknowingly-when he compared the budget of 1975-1976 to the budget of 1985-1986. It was an apples and oranges comparison because there were services in 1975-1976 that were being delivered direct from headquarters, such as education, joint schools capital and child welfare which, now in 1985-1986, are delivered through the region.
1 return to the point that the basis of this whole question is trust. The Minister must advise the House and the country what can now be done to re-establish trust in his Department.

speakeroldname: Hon. Bill McKnight (Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subtopic: INDIAN AFFAIRS-FUNDING OF PROGRAMS. (B) BAND FUNDING INQUIRY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, let me say to my colleague that I appreciate receiving the documents that were delivered by his assistant, although the time was brief for me to look at them. I can tell my colleague that I will be replying to him either in a written form or verbally, after I have had an opportunity to look at those documents. I would say to anyone who has further documentation that I hope they put it forward. I hope it is put into the public realm, either to the Hon. Member or to myself so it can be reviewed.
In the brief time I have, I want to assure the Hon. Member. He has a knowledge of the way our Department works and the way it is funded through 11 different categories of funding. The way that funding has to be handled, we have the ability to adjust within those funding areas, but sometimes there is no ability to adjust.
As the Hon. Member knows, in the Province of Manitoba last year some $2.5 million was returned to Treasury. At the same time there were Supplementary Estimates which went forward for $23.7 million. That is a ratio of $1 to $8. Every dollar which was returned to the Treasury of Canada was replaced with $8. That is the part of the Supplementary Estimates which goes forward across Canada. In Canada a total of some $50 million was returned to the Treasury of Canada. However, at the same time Supplementary Estimates went forward for $140 million plus. In reality, therefore, there was a net gain of some $92 million for Indian programs, for Indian people.
One concern expressed by the Hon. Member in the letter I received today regarded the child welfare agreement and the extension of that existing agreement in the Province of Manitoba. I can assure him that the commitment made by my predecessor that the extension will be funded will be kept. The Hon. Member is accurate. The funds have not been allocated by Cabinet, but I can assure the Hon. Member that the commitment made by my predecessor for the extension of the child welfare agreement in Manitoba will be kept.
I would like to relate to the Hon. Member, to the House and to those in the gallery that the difficulty of allocating funds is
apparent from a conversation I had this morning with the chief of a southern tribal council and some of his advisers who asked if it was possible to move money from welfare to economic development. I said I did not know whether it was possible within my authority. However, the argument made sense. It is much better to use those welfare dollars to provide economic development if the same beneficiaries are going to be working rather than receiving welfare. So while there is criticism and concern about allocation within the Department of Indian Affairs, there is an ongoing pressure from Indian people and Indian governments to make that allocation where it will be effective.
I hope the Hon. Member can wait for my reply to the documents which he provided to me. I can assure him it will be forthcoming in very little time.

subtopic: SUPPLY AND SERVICES-MAINTENANCE CONTRACT FOR F-1S FIGHTER AIRCRAFT. (B) REQUEST FOR TABLING OF CORRESPONDENCE RECEIVED FROM PREMIER OF NOVA SCOTIA
SUPPLY AND SERVICES-MAINTENANCE CONTRACT FOR F-1S FIGHTER AIRCRAFT. (B) REQUEST FOR TABLING OF CORRESPONDENCE RECEIVED FROM PREMIER OF NOVA SCOTIA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise with regard to a question I posed to the Minister of Supply and Services on October 7, 1986. It concerned the awarding of a maintenance contract for the CF-18 fighter aircraft. The substance of my remarks has to do with the principles of fairness and equity for the poorer regions of the country.
I have to say with great sincerity that I was somewhat surprised, if not taken back, by the lack of response given to me at that time by the Minister responsible for Supply and Services. I would have thought that because of the importance of this particular contract, and the potential economic benefits which it could bestow upon a region and upon a people, she would have known of all the considerations being evaluated by her, her Department, and indeed, the entire Cabinet.
There are a number of companies which are bidding for this particular contract. They are western, Quebec and Atlantic consortiums. I thought that the Minister for a very important department, that is, the Department of Supply and Services, would have stood in her place and spelled out the criteria which would be used by the Government of Canada.
We have to put things in perspective when we look at the wording of the contract, since there is much confusion. There is a perception in the country that the Government has already decided, not on the basis of price and the potential of capacity for technical competence, but based on a political promise to a particular Premier of the country.
Let us now consider the contract which Bombardier of Montreal entered into when it purchased the Crown-owned Canadair. Included in that contract to purchase is a clause referring to a royalty payment to the Government of Canada upon the awarding of the CF-18 contract to Canadair. The royalty represents approximately 1 per cent of the total contract price. The federal Government agreed to this clause
October 9, 1986

even though potential buyers were advised that the award was not to be considered a component of the Canadair sale. Upon signing, the Government committed itself to this agreement. This is inconsistent with the procedure of the Department of Supply and Services and can be viewed by some as an inducement.
Then there is talk about the bid being submitted from Atlantic Canada. The Minister, but more particularly her colleagues from Nova Scotia, have been extremely silent with respect to the inducements and previous decisions they had taken in the months prior.
Atlantic Canada was set adrift in November of 1984 as a result of the financial statement made by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson). Because of the outcry from Atlantic Canadians, First Ministers, members of the Opposition, as well as members of the Tory caucus, a decision was reached by the Government, as announced by the Minister's predecessor in February of 1986, which talked about the procurement of goods and services by the Government of Canada. Is this to be considered in the awarding of this contract?
The Government then said that it wanted to increase significantly-to the tune of $600 million over five years-the goods and services going into Atlantic Canada in order to enable businesses in that region of the country to gain some advantage. This is a clear and unequivocal opportunity to live up to the commitment of some months ago. However, all of a sudden the Government is very silent. It does not want to say anything. Ministers from Halifax and Central Nova have become sick. They cannot speak any longer about a program which they introduced with great fanfare. Nor does the Minister make reference to it in response to the question I asked. Perhaps today we will receive a different answer.
The Premier of Nova Scotia who extolled the virtues of this new-found policy of procurement has been silent. It is not something which has been legislated like it ought to have been. When I asked the Minister in a spirit of openness with respect to what those representations were and whether or not she would table them, I again received silence.
A reasonable person such as you, Mr. Speaker, would conclude that someone is hiding something here. One is left to conclude that there is something under the table when no reference is made to previous policies which have been announced, when Ministers who would normally speak up for their regions are extremely silent and when a provincial Premier is as silent as a mouse. I find the whole bidding procedure with regard to this particular contract to be very questionable.
I hope the Minister will avail herself of the opportunity to address this situation and to give an undertaking that all regions of the country, including Atlantic Canada, will have an equal and fair opportunity to bid for government contracts. We will not suffer prejudice because we come from a slow-
Adjournment Debate
growth area. I hope the Minister can provide that undertaking not only to me as an Atlantic Member of Parliament but to Canadians who live in that part of Canada and who subscribe to a Canadian Constitution that speaks directly about equality of opportunity.

speakeroldname: Hon. Monique Vezina (Minister of Supply and Services):
subtopic: SUPPLY AND SERVICES-MAINTENANCE CONTRACT FOR F-1S FIGHTER AIRCRAFT. (B) REQUEST FOR TABLING OF CORRESPONDENCE RECEIVED FROM PREMIER OF NOVA SCOTIA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to thank the Hon. Member for Cape Breton-Richmond East (Mr. Dingwall) for giving me an opportunity to raise this important question once again, an issue on which, as I said recently, emotions have been running high.
Mr. Speaker, exactly what is covered by this contract? It means that the technical and engineering maintenance of CF-18 fighters used by our armed forces can now be done in this country. Until now, this service was provided by the MacDon-nell-Douglas Corporation of St. Louis, in the United States. From the outset, it was intended that this maintenance service would eventually be done in Canada.
At the request of the Department of National Defence, my Department started the process of repatriating this service. The first step was to inform 16 Canadian companies in the aerospace industry of what we intended to do. As always in this kind of situation, a number of groups or consortiums were formed. These groups, which are known to the public, are the consortia formed around IMP of Halifax, Bristol of Winnipeg and Canadair of Montreal.
The groups prepared and presented proposals which were then subject to careful scrutiny. However, I hardly think the Hon. Member expects me to reveal the results of this assessment this evening.
According to our regulations, it was then up to the Minister of Supply and Services to transmit the results of the assessment and his conclusions to Treasury Board. And that is what I have done, Mr. Speaker. And, as was mentioned several times, the entire matter is now being examined by Treasury Board, in preparation for a meeting of Treasury Board Ministers who will have to make a decision.
Recently, the Hon. Member asked me what the criteria would be for their decision.
Mr. Speaker, a great many factors are involved. There is the technical assessment, price, offsets in terms of jobs, technology transfers and, finally, economic impact.
Mr. Speaker, the decision is a very difficult one. As Ministers, it is our responsibility to analyse all relevant factors to the best of our ability and to make a decision in terms of what we consider to be Canada's national interest. That is what we will do.
Mr. Speaker, I have one last comment to make. As you know, and as this House and all Canadian men and women know, the issue of which consortium will get the contract has become a very emotional one, and I deplore that. Neither emotions nor partisan considerations will determine who will

October 9, 1986
Adjournment Debate
get the contract. What will determine the outcome will be a rational assessment by Ministers representing all Canadian regions. Unlike our predecessors, we belong to a truly national, not a regional party.
Mr. Speaker, the balances existing within our Government strengthen my conviction that our decision, whatever it may be, will be in the best interests of this country.
